title: General Skolem problem
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Given a linear recurrence sequence with rational coefficients and rational initial values, decide whether any term is zero. A solution must terminate on every input, not merely enumerate zero terms or settle restricted spectral configurations.
status: Originates in work surrounding the Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem in the twentieth century. Substantial conditional decidability results exist, but unconditional general decidability remains unresolved.
why: Settles a fundamental obstruction to exact reachability analysis for linear programs.
key_works: Bilu et al. (2022), *Skolem Meets Schanuel*, arXiv:2204.13417, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2022.20; Lipton et al. (2022), *On the Skolem Problem and the Skolem Conjecture*, DOI:10.1145/3531130.3533328.
aliases: Zero-occurrence problem for linear recurrence sequences.

title: Skolem problem at order five
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Decide zero occurrence for every rational linear recurrence sequence of order five. The difficult configurations include simple recurrences with two dominant complex-conjugate pairs of equal modulus and a smaller real root.
status: Orders at most four are decidable. Numerous order-five configurations are settled, but the complete order-five problem remains open in the 2026 survey.
why: Resolves the first remaining dimensional boundary rather than the unrestricted problem.
key_works: Lipton et al. (2022), *On the Skolem Problem and the Skolem Conjecture*, DOI:10.1145/3531130.3533328; Bacik et al. (2026), *A Survey of the Skolem and Positivity Problems for Linear Recurrence Sequences*.

title: Positivity at order six
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Decide whether every term of an arbitrary rational linear recurrence sequence of order six is nonnegative.
status: Positivity is decidable through order five. Order six remains a first unresolved boundary and encounters difficult Diophantine-approximation questions.
why: Enables exact verification of persistent inequalities in low-dimensional linear loops.
key_works: Bacik, Karimov, Luca, Nieuwveld, Ouaknine, Purser, and Worrell (2026), *A Survey of the Skolem and Positivity Problems for Linear Recurrence Sequences*, especially its low-order positivity discussion.

title: Ultimate positivity for nonsimple order-six recurrences
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Decide whether every sufficiently late term of an order-six rational recurrence is nonnegative when repeated characteristic roots are allowed.
status: Ultimate positivity for simple recurrences is decidable at arbitrary order; that solved result does not settle nonsimple order-six sequences.
why: Determines eventual safety after a finite transient.
key_works: Bacik et al. (2026), *A Survey of the Skolem and Positivity Problems for Linear Recurrence Sequences*, sections on ultimate positivity and repeated roots.

title: Positivity for simple order-ten recurrences
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Decide nonnegativity of all terms of every simple rational linear recurrence sequence of order ten.
status: The simple case is decidable through order nine. The order-ten boundary remains unresolved and is connected to order-five Skolem instances.
why: Extends exact safety checking beyond the present simple-recurrence boundary.
key_works: Bacik et al. (2026), *A Survey of the Skolem and Positivity Problems for Linear Recurrence Sequences*, discussion of simple positivity and its order-ten obstruction.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time low-order Skolem algorithms
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Obtain deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for the low-order Skolem cases currently supported by randomized complexity bounds, with bit complexity measured in the binary input size.
status: Decidability at order at most four is established; the complexity frontier includes coRP algorithms. Removing randomness is a separate problem from proving decidability.
why: Produces predictable, reproducible arithmetic decision procedures.
key_works: Bacik, Ouaknine, Purser, and Worrell (2026), *On the p-adic Skolem Problem*, arXiv:2504.14413, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.STACS.2026.8; the maintained SKOLEM project and its research references.

title: Bounded continuous Skolem problem
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Given a rational linear differential system, a rational observation vector, and a bounded rational time interval, decide whether the observed trajectory is exactly zero anywhere in that interval.
status: Unconditional decidability is unresolved in general. Conditional procedures and substantial special cases exist; numerical approximation alone does not decide exact tangential zeros.
why: Addresses exact event detection in linear continuous-system verification.
key_works: Chonev, Ouaknine, and Worrell (2015/2016), *On the Skolem Problem for Continuous Linear Dynamical Systems*, arXiv:1506.00695.

title: Unbounded continuous Skolem problem
subfield: Linear recurrences and arithmetic dynamical systems
open: Decide whether a linear differential-system observation reaches zero at any nonnegative real time, without imposing a finite horizon.
status: Restricted frequency configurations admit reductions or algorithms. The unrestricted problem remains tied to difficult effective Diophantine-approximation questions.
why: Supports unbounded-time reachability and safety arguments for linear plants.
key_works: Bell, Delvenne, Jungers, and Blondel (2010), *The Continuous Skolem-Pisot Problem*, arXiv:0809.2189; Chonev, Ouaknine, and Worrell, arXiv:1506.00695.

title: Polynomial-time parity games
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: Give a rigorously validated polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary finite parity games, or establish an appropriate complexity-theoretic obstruction.
status: Quasipolynomial algorithms are established. A November 2025 preprint claims polynomial time, but I found no independent validation; 2026 research still describes polynomial-time solvability as unresolved.
why: Would improve a central algorithmic foundation of reactive synthesis and temporal verification.
key_works: Fearnley et al. (2017), *An Ordered Approach to Solving Parity Games in Quasi Polynomial Time and Quasi Linear Space*, arXiv:1703.01296; van der Heijden (2025), *Attractors Is All You Need*, arXiv:2511.03752, **unvalidated claim**; Chen, Li, and Yannakakis (2026), arXiv:2604.00268.

title: Polynomial-time mean-payoff games
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: Decide the winner of a finite two-player mean-payoff game in time polynomial in the graph size and binary weight encoding.
status: Pseudopolynomial and improved structural algorithms exist; a general polynomial-time algorithm remains unresolved.
why: Enables efficient synthesis with long-run resource, energy, and performance objectives.
key_works: Fijalkow et al. (2020), *Value Iteration Using Universal Graphs and the Complexity of Mean Payoff Games*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2020.34; Chen et al. (2026), arXiv:2604.00268.

title: Polynomial-time simple stochastic games
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: Compute, or compare against a rational threshold, the exact reachability value of an arbitrary simple stochastic game in polynomial time.
status: The general complexity question remains open despite extensive strategy-iteration, value-iteration, and reduction research.
why: Improves adversarial probabilistic verification and controller synthesis.
key_works: Chen, Li, and Yannakakis (2026), *The Mystery Deepens: On the Query Complexity of Tarski Fixed Points*, arXiv:2604.00268; Berthon, Katoen, and Zhou (2025), *A Direct Reduction from Stochastic Parity Games to Simple Stochastic Games*.

title: Uniformly efficient discounted stochastic games
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: Obtain algorithms for finite turn-based discounted stochastic games whose polynomial guarantees remain effective when discount factors are part of the input and approach one.
status: Fixed-discount and structured cases do not resolve the uniform complexity frontier. Discounted stochastic games remain part of the unresolved game/fixed-point complexity landscape.
why: Prevents verification cost from exploding for long-horizon discounted objectives.
key_works: Chen, Li, and Yannakakis (2026), *The Mystery Deepens: On the Query Complexity of Tarski Fixed Points*, arXiv:2604.00268.

title: Polynomial-time ARRIVAL
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: Decide in polynomial time whether the deterministic switching walk of an ARRIVAL instance reaches its designated destination.
status: ARRIVAL is in NP∩coNP, with subexponential algorithms. The 2025 recursive framework improves structural understanding but does not settle membership in P.
why: Clarifies the complexity of deceptively simple deterministic transition systems.
key_works: Haslebacher (2025), *ARRIVAL: Recursive Framework & ℓ₁-Contraction*, arXiv:2502.06477, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.95.

title: Tight higher-dimensional Tarski query bounds
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: Determine matching upper and lower bounds for finding a fixed point of a monotone map on a finite grid in each fixed dimension above four.
status: The four-dimensional query bound was tightened to order log²n in 2026. Higher dimensions retain gaps between known upper and lower bounds.
why: Explains the intrinsic cost of black-box fixed-point computations underlying verification.
key_works: Chen, Li, and Yannakakis (2026), *The Mystery Deepens: On the Query Complexity of Tarski Fixed Points*, arXiv:2604.00268.

title: Tenfold faster independently certified parity solving
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: On a frozen diverse benchmark suite, reduce total solving-plus-independent-checking time by at least 10× while retaining explicit winning-strategy certificates for both players.
status: Proposed engineering target. Existing quasipolynomial, attractor, and strategy-based algorithms offer different practical trade-offs; asymptotic improvement alone does not establish this target.
why: Converts algorithmic progress into trustworthy synthesis throughput.
key_works: Fearnley et al. (2017), arXiv:1703.01296; Di Stasio, Murano, Perelli, and Vardi (2019), *Solving Parity Games Using an Automata-Based Algorithm*, arXiv:1910.13765.

title: Numerically reliable stochastic-game stopping criteria
subfield: Games, fixed points, and algorithmic complexity
open: Build exact or certified-interval stochastic-game solvers that return sound termination certificates even near value ties and under floating-point roundoff.
status: Sound value-iteration approaches exist. The remaining target combines large instances, tight error guarantees, independently checked certificates, and predictable termination behavior.
why: Prevents apparently converged numerical values from becoming unsound verification results.
key_works: Quatmann and Katoen (2018), *Sound Value Iteration*; Dehnert et al. (2017), *A Storm Is Coming*, arXiv:1702.04311.

title: Exact complexity of three-dimensional VASS reachability
open: Close the complexity gap for reachability in three-dimensional vector addition systems with states.
status: The 2025 result proves an elementary upper bound: 2EXPSPACE membership, against PSPACE hardness. “Is 3-VASS reachability elementary?” is therefore no longer open.
why: Locates a sharp low-dimensional boundary in counter-system verification.
key_works: Czerwiński, Jecker, Lasota, and Orlikowski (2025), *Reachability in 3-VASS Is Elementary*, arXiv:2502.13916, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.153.

title: Practical certified VASS reachability witnesses
open: Develop compressed witness formats and small verified checkers that make large counter-system reachability proofs usable without expanding enormous execution sequences.
status: Decidability and recent low-dimensional bounds are major theoretical achievements; they do not automatically provide practical certificate pipelines.
why: Makes difficult infinite-state results inspectable and reusable in software verification.
key_works: Czerwiński et al. (2025), *Reachability in 3-VASS Is Elementary*, arXiv:2502.13916.

title: Cutoffs for dynamically changing populations
open: Derive sound, computable cutoffs for useful classes of protocols whose participants join, leave, and change roles, with explicit restrictions that avoid known undecidability.
status: Parameterized verification has strong results for structured process families and threshold automata. Dynamic membership requires additional reasoning beyond fixed-population abstractions.
why: Supports proofs that survive autoscaling and membership changes.
key_works: Konnov, Lazić, Stoilkovska, and Widder (2020), *Survey on Parameterized Verification with Threshold Automata and the Byzantine Model Checker*, arXiv:2011.14789.

title: Parameterized Byzantine liveness with changing quorums
open: Mechanize liveness proofs for threshold protocols combining dynamic quorums, adaptive faults, and explicitly bounded synchrony assumptions across all admissible system sizes.
status: Threshold-automata methods already address substantial Byzantine verification problems. This combined setting is a narrower extension target, not a claim that Byzantine verification is absent.
why: Reduces reliance on small-instance checks for operationally changing consensus systems.
key_works: Konnov et al. (2020), arXiv:2011.14789; Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet: Proving Safety and Liveness of Practical Distributed Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3068608.

title: Exact parameter regions for realistic timed models
open: Compute certified admissible timing-parameter regions for industrial-sized models containing scheduling, bounded queues, and clock uncertainty, with termination guarantees on a declared model class.
status: Parametric timed verification has decidable fragments and useful tools; unrestricted parameter synthesis cannot simply be assumed decidable.
why: Replaces trial-and-error timeout selection with proved operating envelopes.
key_works: André (2019), *Parametric Verification: An Introduction*, arXiv:1907.00555.

title: Robustness-preserving timed abstraction
open: Construct abstractions whose certificates transfer timing properties under explicitly quantified clock drift, measurement error, and implementation jitter.
status: Exact-clock timed verification and parametric analysis provide foundations. A useful solution must prove robustness margins rather than merely rerun analysis at sampled parameter values.
why: Bridges ideal timed automata and deployed clocks.
key_works: André (2019), arXiv:1907.00555; Pinisetty et al. (2012), *Runtime Enforcement of Timed Properties*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-35632-2_23.

title: Unbounded recursive-concurrent verification beyond fixed context bounds
open: Identify useful program classes admitting compositional, terminating verification procedures without fixing a global thread-context-switch bound.
status: Thread-modular analyses and compositional logics provide partial answers. The target is an expressive decidable or effectively checkable fragment, not unrestricted concurrent-program decidability.
why: Avoids confusing bounded concurrency exploration with an unbounded guarantee.
key_works: *Effect Summaries for Thread-Modular Analysis* (2017), arXiv:1705.03701; Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*.

title: Replayable infinite-state liveness counterexamples
open: Produce finite, independently checkable descriptions of genuine nontermination or fairness violations in infinite-state systems, distinguishing them from abstraction artifacts.
status: Finite-state lasso witnesses are standard; counter systems and recursive programs require richer summaries and explicit fairness semantics.
why: Turns failed liveness proofs into actionable diagnostics.
key_works: D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*, DOI:10.1145/3477082; Czerwiński et al. (2025), arXiv:2502.13916.

title: Word equations with linear length constraints
open: Decide satisfiability of word equations over a finite alphabet combined with linear constraints on string lengths.
status: This remains a longstanding decidability question, explicitly discussed as open in 2026 work. Decidability of word equations alone does not settle the combination.
why: Addresses a foundational limit of string verification for parsers and web applications.
key_works: Ganesh et al. (2013), *(Un)Decidability Results for Word Equations with Length and Regular Expression Constraints*, arXiv:1306.6054; Przybocki and Barrett (2026), DOI:10.1007/978-3-032-32592-1_14.

title: Quadratic word equations with length constraints
open: Settle decidability for the general quadratic fragment, where each variable occurs at most twice, combined with linear length constraints.
status: Important subclasses are decidable. The general quadratic combination remains open; recent two-variable results should not be mistaken for a solution of the whole fragment.
why: Targets a restricted string-theory boundary with direct solver relevance.
key_works: Lin and Majumdar (2021), *Quadratic Word Equations with Length Constraints, Counter Systems, and Presburger Arithmetic with Divisibility*, arXiv:2007.15478; Przybocki and Barrett (2026), DOI:10.1007/978-3-032-32592-1_14.

title: Complete termination criteria for Nielsen-based string solving
open: Characterize the residual word-equation classes for which Nielsen transformations terminate when length information is propagated, beyond currently established cut-graph criteria.
status: The 2026 analysis supplies sufficient conditions and necessity for substantial classes; it does not close every remaining termination case.
why: Converts heuristic string solvers into procedures with explicit termination envelopes.
key_works: Przybocki and Barrett (2026), *The Termination of Nielsen Transformations Applied to Word Equations with Length Constraints*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-032-32592-1_14.

title: Complete SMT proof coverage without trusted solver escape hatches
open: Make every successful result in a declared, practically broad SMT fragment export a proof accepted by a small independently maintained checker, including preprocessing.
status: Alethe and Carcara establish important infrastructure. Coverage, elaboration cost, and treatment of complex theory steps remain separate engineering obligations.
why: Shrinks the trusted base of verification tools using SMT.
key_works: Andreotti, Lachnitt, and Barbosa (2023), *Carcara: An Efficient Proof Checker and Elaborator for SMT Proofs in the Alethe Format*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-30823-9_19.

title: Independently checked transcendental SMT certificates
open: Produce practical certificates for nonlinear real constraints involving elementary transcendental functions, explicitly distinguishing exact results from δ-complete guarantees.
status: dReal provides δ-complete approaches; certified approximation systems address portions of the numerical foundation. Exact unrestricted transcendental decision procedures are not assumed possible.
why: Makes nonlinear verification trustworthy without concealing approximation semantics.
key_works: Gao, Avigad, and Clarke (2012), *Delta-Complete Decision Procedures for Satisfiability over the Reals*; Gao, Kong, and Clarke (2013), *dReal*.

title: Stable quantified SMT reasoning for evolving specifications
open: Develop quantifier-instantiation and proof-repair methods whose success is robust to semantics-preserving changes such as declaration reordering, harmless auxiliary lemmas, and renaming.
status: SMT-backed verification is effective, but solver sensitivity is a documented proof-engineering concern. The target requires longitudinal mutation tests, not a single benchmark score.
why: Prevents verification pipelines from becoming brittle under ordinary development.
key_works: Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*, DOI:10.1561/2500000045; Why3 project, maintained verification-platform documentation.

title: Scalable mixed floating-point and bit-vector certificates
open: Certify large mixed IEEE floating-point, bit-vector, and memory queries without either enormous bit-blasted proofs or unverifiable specialized reasoning.
status: Bit-level encodings and numerical certificate checkers solve important pieces. Efficient composition of these proof styles is the remaining target.
why: Supports low-level numerical software and hardware verification.
key_works: Becker et al. (2018), *A Verified Certificate Checker for Finite-Precision Error Bounds in Coq and HOL4*, arXiv:1707.02115; Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*.

title: Incremental SMT certificates with sound scope management
open: Design compact proof logs for incremental solving that preserve dependencies across push/pop, assumptions, preprocessing, and shared learned lemmas.
status: General proof formats and checkers exist. The proposed target is reliable cross-session reuse without accepting lemmas outside the assumptions that justify them.
why: Allows cached verification work without introducing stale-proof unsoundness.
key_works: *Alethe: Towards a Generic SMT Proof Format* (2021), HAL:hal-03341413; Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-30823-9_19.

title: Superpolynomial Frege lower bounds
open: Exhibit an explicit family of propositional tautologies requiring superpolynomial-size proofs in general Frege systems.
status: A longstanding central proof-complexity problem. Strong lower bounds for weaker systems do not extend automatically to unrestricted Frege.
why: Explains intrinsic limitations of powerful propositional proof engines.
key_works: Razborov (2023), *Propositional Proof Complexity*, EMS chapter; Beame and Pitassi, *Propositional Proof Complexity: Past, Present, and Future*.

title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
open: Prove superpolynomial proof-size lower bounds for an explicit tautology family in Extended Frege, allowing extension variables that abbreviate formulas.
status: Remains open despite decades of progress for weaker systems. Extension variables make this substantially stronger than many familiar lower-bound settings.
why: Tests the limits of proof systems resembling reusable intermediate reasoning.
key_works: Razborov (2023), *Propositional Proof Complexity*; *Meta-Mathematics of Computational Complexity Theory* (2025), arXiv:2504.04416.

title: Strong lower bounds for bounded-depth Frege with modular counting
open: Establish superpolynomial lower bounds for appropriate explicit tautologies in bounded-depth Frege systems augmented with modular counting gates, such as AC⁰[p]-Frege.
status: Ordinary bounded-depth lower bounds do not settle the modular-counting extensions. These stronger systems remain important barriers.
why: Separates the power of counting principles from weaker propositional reasoning.
key_works: Razborov (2023), *Propositional Proof Complexity*, discussion of bounded-depth systems with modular connectives.

title: Existence of p-optimal propositional proof systems
open: Decide whether a propositional proof system exists that polynomially simulates every other propositional proof system.
status: The p-optimality question remains unresolved. It is distinct from whether some proof system has polynomial-size proofs of every tautology.
why: Determines whether there could be a universally efficient proof representation, up to polynomial overhead.
key_works: *Meta-Mathematics of Computational Complexity Theory* (2025), arXiv:2504.04416; Razborov (2023), *Propositional Proof Complexity*.

title: General algebraic proof-system lower bounds
open: Prove superpolynomial lower bounds for explicit instances in powerful algebraic proof systems whose certificates are represented by unrestricted arithmetic circuits.
status: Restricted algebraic proof models have significant lower bounds; unrestricted circuit representations encounter major algebraic-complexity barriers.
why: Clarifies whether algebraic certificates can evade conventional propositional bottlenecks.
key_works: Pitassi (2016), *Algebraic Proof Complexity: Progress, Frontiers and Challenges*; Razborov (2023), *Propositional Proof Complexity*.

title: Scalable certification of distributed SAT solving
open: Certify parallel SAT solving with dynamically shared clauses, worker failures, and proof merging while keeping checking substantially cheaper than rediscovering the proof.
status: Verified SAT-certificate checkers exist. Distributed provenance and efficient global proof assembly remain additional targets.
why: Makes large parallel verification workloads independently trustworthy.
key_works: Tan et al. (2021), *cake_lpr: Verified Propagation Redundancy Checking*, associated primary paper and artifact; CakeML project.

title: Hundredfold smaller proof logs without trust expansion
open: Reduce stored SAT/SMT certificate volume by at least 100× on a preregistered large-instance suite while preserving independent checking and accounting for reconstruction cost.
status: Proposed moonshot. Existing proof formats, elaboration, and verified checking supply baselines; compression alone is insufficient if checking becomes impractical.
why: Makes proof retention feasible for continuous verification at scale.
key_works: Tan et al. (2021), *cake_lpr*; Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-30823-9_19.

title: Proof-carrying solver portfolios
open: Build portfolios that combine SAT, SMT, abstract interpretation, and numerical reasoning while exporting one checked argument covering every cross-engine assumption.
status: Individual certificate systems exist; trusting each solver independently does not establish the soundness of their orchestration.
why: Enables heterogeneous automation without a correspondingly large trusted base.
key_works: Chihani, Miller, and Renaud, *Foundational Proof Certificates in First-Order Logic*; Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*.

title: Automatically synthesized abstract domains with checked soundness
open: Generate problem-specific abstract domains and transfer functions automatically, accompanied by machine-checked soundness proofs and measured precision/cost trade-offs.
status: Abstract interpretation supplies the foundational framework; the proposed target is automated domain construction that remains useful on changing real programs.
why: Reduces the expert effort needed to create effective static analyses.
key_works: Cousot and Cousot (1977), *Abstract Interpretation: A Unified Lattice Model for Static Analysis of Programs by Construction or Approximation of Fixpoints*, DOI:10.1145/512950.512973.

title: Predictably precise widening
open: Construct widening strategies with explicit, checkable precision-loss explanations and robust behavior under equivalent program transformations.
status: Widening solves convergence problems but introduces analysis-dependent approximation. No universal optimality is assumed; the target is predictable behavior on declared domain families.
why: Makes false alarms understandable and analysis results more stable.
key_works: Cousot and Cousot (1977), DOI:10.1145/512950.512973; Cousot, *Abstract Interpretation in a Nutshell*.

title: Certified relational heap-and-numerical analysis
open: Combine heap shape, aliasing, arithmetic relationships, and concurrency permissions in an analyzer whose reductions between domains are formally proved sound.
status: Shape analyses, numerical domains, and separation logics each provide strong components. Their scalable, automatically tuned combination remains an engineering frontier.
why: Targets bugs that disappear when heap and arithmetic facts are analyzed separately.
key_works: Cousot and Cousot (1977); Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*.

title: Reusable IC3 invariants across program revisions
open: Reuse property-directed reachability clauses after code changes while proving which clauses remain valid and efficiently repairing invalidated dependencies.
status: IC3/PDR established effective incremental inductive reasoning. Cross-revision proof reuse requires stronger dependency management than ordinary within-run incrementality.
why: Reduces continuous-verification costs.
key_works: Bradley (2012), *Understanding IC3*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-31612-8_1; Palmskog, Celik, and Gligoric (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*.

title: Explainable failed invariant generalization
open: Make model checkers explain why candidate invariants fail, distinguishing genuine missing state, abstraction imprecision, and insufficient induction strength.
status: IC3 and related methods generate and refine inductive clauses; the proposed target is a validated diagnostic interface rather than another opaque heuristic.
why: Helps developers repair specifications and abstractions instead of blindly tuning solvers.

title: Compositional verification of data-dependent resource bounds
open: Infer and certify useful time, allocation, and energy bounds for programs combining recursion, mutable structures, and input-dependent control flow.
status: Verified language implementations and program logics offer components; the combined target must expose hardware and cost-model assumptions.
why: Extends correctness beyond “does not crash” to operational feasibility.
key_works: CakeML project, verified compiler and cost-related verification work; Cousot, *Abstract Interpretation in a Nutshell*.

title: Confidence-aware analysis without weakening soundness claims
open: Integrate statistical confidence with static analysis while clearly separating proved absence of bugs, probabilistic claims under a distribution, and heuristic alarm rankings.
status: PLDI 2026 work develops foundations for confidence-aware abstract interpretation. Calibration under distribution shift and integration with conventional sound analyses remain extension targets.
why: Prevents probabilistic prioritization from being mislabeled as universal verification.
key_works: *Abstract Interpretation with Confidence* (PLDI 2026), conference paper and presentation.

title: Tenfold cheaper whole-program safety analysis
open: Achieve at least a 10× reduction in total analysis cost on a frozen multi-language corpus while preserving a declared soundness envelope and false-alarm rate.
status: Proposed benchmarked moonshot; comparisons must include annotation labor, memory, and incremental reruns rather than solver time alone.
why: Makes sound analysis practical for more development workflows.
key_works: Cousot and Cousot (1977); Huang et al. (2026), *Lessons from Formally Verified Deployed Software Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3785652.

title: Small controllers from expressive temporal specifications
open: Synthesize controllers that are simultaneously correct, compact, and operationally efficient for large expressive temporal specifications, with independent strategy checking.
status: LTL synthesis and competitions are established; controller size and implementation quality remain distinct objectives from realizability.
why: Makes synthesized controllers deployable rather than merely mathematically available.
key_works: Křetínský et al. (2026), *SemML 2.0: Synthesizing Controllers for LTL*, arXiv:2604.24102; SYNTCOMP, 2026 competition resources.

title: Minimal nonvacuous environment assumptions
open: Infer environment assumptions that make a specification realizable while avoiding assumptions that exclude the intended deployment or trivialize the guarantee.
status: Assumption engineering is fundamental to synthesis; the target requires explicit minimality criteria and independently reviewed environment relevance.
why: Prevents correct controllers for impossible or irrelevant worlds.
key_works: SYNTCOMP specification and benchmark resources; Křetínský et al. (2026), *SemML 2.0*, arXiv:2604.24102.

title: Incremental synthesis under requirement changes
open: Update a synthesized controller after localized specification changes, preserving unaffected guarantees and generating a compact proof of the modification.
status: Modern synthesis tools provide strong one-shot baselines. The proposed target measures cumulative cost and behavioral disruption over realistic revision histories.
why: Allows synthesis to participate in ordinary iterative development.
key_works: Křetínský et al. (2026), arXiv:2604.24102; Palmskog et al. (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*.

title: Useful decidable distributed-synthesis fragments
open: Identify and implement expressive architectural restrictions permitting distributed synthesis with partial information, rather than attempting the known-undecidable unrestricted problem.
status: Centralized synthesis progress does not eliminate information-flow barriers in distributed settings.
why: Supports synthesis of cooperating services and embedded components.
key_works: SYNTCOMP resources; Seshia, Sadigh, and Sastry (2022), *Towards Verified Artificial Intelligence*, arXiv:1606.08514.

title: Scalable alternating-quantifier hyperproperty checking
open: Verify useful properties with alternating quantification over executions, while producing checked certificates and avoiding explicit construction of prohibitively large self-products.
status: Hyperproperty verification extends ordinary trace checking, but quantifier alternation and system size create substantial scaling challenges.
why: Supports security and refinement statements that compare multiple possible executions.
key_works: *HyperProb: A Model Checker for Probabilistic Hyperproperties* (2021), DOI:10.1007/978-3-030-90870-6_35; *Model-Checking HyperLTL for Pushdown Systems*, HAL:hal-03902458.

title: Hyperproperty-preserving abstraction
open: Develop abstractions with explicit preservation theorems for selected combinations of universal and existential trace quantifiers, nondeterminism, and probability.
status: Ordinary safety-preserving abstraction does not automatically preserve relational properties. Existing hyperproperty tools supply narrower baselines.
why: Makes compositional security analysis sound.

title: Quantitative synthesis with deployable resource guarantees
open: Synthesize controllers satisfying logical requirements and certified limits on memory, energy, intervention frequency, and response latency.
status: Quantitative games and multiobjective methods address components; simultaneously connecting their objectives to implementation-level resource costs remains open engineering work.
why: Prevents formally correct but operationally unusable controllers.
key_works: Bruyère et al. (2019), *Energy Mean-Payoff Games*, arXiv:1907.01359; Delgrange et al. (2020), *Simple Strategies in Multi-Objective MDPs*.

title: Tenfold synthesis improvement with proof-producing learned heuristics
open: Achieve a reproducible 10× end-to-end improvement over a frozen synthesis baseline using learned search guidance, while independently checking every returned controller.
status: Learning-guided synthesis is already demonstrated; the proposed target requires generalization across specification families and includes unsuccessful runs.
why: Uses learning to improve search without trusting learned correctness judgments.
key_works: *SemML: Enhancing Automata-Theoretic LTL Synthesis* (2025), arXiv:2501.17496; Křetínský et al. (2026), *SemML 2.0*, arXiv:2604.24102.

title: Certified almost-sure termination for nonlinear probabilistic loops
open: Automatically synthesize machine-checkable almost-sure termination arguments for useful nonlinear probabilistic programs with unbounded state.
status: Martingales, expectation invariants, and specialized analyses provide partial methods; universal completeness is not claimed.
why: Establishes that randomized software actually finishes with probability one.
key_works: Chakarov and Sankaranarayanan (2014), *Expectation Invariants for Probabilistic Program Loops as Fixed Points*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-10936-7_6; *Polynomial Probabilistic Invariants and the Optional Stopping Theorem* (2019), arXiv:1910.12634.

title: Tight certified expected-runtime bounds
open: Infer useful upper and lower expected-runtime bounds, not merely termination, for probabilistic loops with state-dependent distributions and nested recursion.
status: Expectation-based program analyses exist. Tightness, automation, and applicability to realistic recursive programs remain separate targets.
why: Connects probabilistic correctness to cost and service-level planning.
key_works: Chakarov and Sankaranarayanan (2014), DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-10936-7_6; *Polynomial Probabilistic Invariants and the Optional Stopping Theorem*, arXiv:1910.12634.

title: Sound automatic use of optional stopping
open: Automatically verify the side conditions needed for optional-stopping arguments, including integrability and boundedness conditions, and reject invalid probabilistic proofs.
status: The theorem is established; identifying and proving its applicability inside automated program verification remains the target.
why: Prevents elegant but invalid martingale arguments.
key_works: *Polynomial Probabilistic Invariants and the Optional Stopping Theorem* (2019), arXiv:1910.12634.

title: Proof certificates for learned probabilistic invariants
open: Combine data-driven invariant discovery with independent symbolic validation that covers all relevant states rather than only sampled executions.
status: Data-driven probabilistic invariant learning has demonstrated progress; the remaining target is reliable certificate production under distribution and program changes.
why: Uses statistical discovery without converting sampling success into a false universal guarantee.
key_works: Bao et al. (2025), *Data-Driven Invariant Learning for Probabilistic Programs*, DOI:10.1007/s10703-024-00466-x.

title: Practical indefinite-horizon POMDP verification
open: Produce tight certified bounds for large partially observable models over indefinite horizons, including explicit gaps when exact solutions are unavailable.
status: Indefinite-horizon POMDP verification methods exist; scaling belief-state reasoning and closing bounds remain active targets.
why: Supports agents and controllers that cannot directly observe the complete state.
key_works: Bork, Junges, Katoen, and Quatmann (2020), *Verification of Indefinite-Horizon POMDPs*; Storm publications.

title: Probabilistic certificates robust to model uncertainty
open: Verify guarantees over explicitly defined uncertainty sets for transition probabilities, while accounting for uncertainty-set estimation and finite data.
status: Probabilistic model checking assumes a model; statistical estimation and formal verification must be connected rather than conflated.
why: Makes numerical guarantees meaningful when probabilities are learned from observations.
key_works: Dehnert et al. (2017), *A Storm Is Coming*, arXiv:1702.04311; Seshia et al. (2022), *Towards Verified Artificial Intelligence*, arXiv:1606.08514.

title: Certified rare-event probabilities at practical cost
open: Estimate or bound extremely small failure probabilities using variance reduction while providing independently checkable justification for bias control and confidence coverage.
status: Numerical model checking and statistical methods provide foundations; very rare events make naive simulation inadequate and model assumptions especially consequential.
why: Supports reliability claims about failures unlikely to appear during ordinary testing.
key_works: *The Probabilistic Model Checker Storm* (2021), DOI:10.1007/s10009-021-00633-z; PRISM project documentation.

title: Compositional multiobjective probability bounds
open: Compose verified components while retaining useful joint bounds on failure probability, expected cost, and deadline satisfaction, including dependence between components.
status: Multiobjective MDP and Markov-automata methods exist; scalable composition without unjustified independence assumptions remains a distinct challenge.
why: Prevents individually acceptable components from producing an unacceptable system.
key_works: Quatmann, Junges, and Katoen (2017), *Markov Automata with Multiple Objectives*; Hartmanns et al. (2018), *Multi-Cost Bounded Reachability in MDP*.

title: Detecting vacuous industrial specifications
open: Automatically detect when a proved property is satisfied only because assumptions are inconsistent, preconditions exclude intended use, or the postcondition omits the relevant behavior.
status: Mutation analysis and specification testing provide partial evidence; proof success itself does not establish adequacy.
why: Addresses “proved the wrong thing” failures.
key_works: Celik et al. (2019), *Mutation Analysis for Coq*; Jain et al. (2020), *mCoq: Mutation Analysis for Coq Verification Projects*.

title: Requirement-to-formal-specification fidelity
open: Build a workflow that exposes ambiguities, records stakeholder resolutions, and tests whether a formal specification faithfully represents an independently written requirement.
status: Proposed scoped target, not a universal solution to informal meaning. Existing formal verification establishes conformance to formal specifications, not automatic correctness of the specification choice.
why: Connects mathematical assurance to actual user intent.
key_works: Clarke and Wing et al. (1996), *Formal Methods: State of the Art and Future Directions*, DOI:10.1145/242223.242257; Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652.

title: Usable semantic coverage metrics
open: Define and validate metrics measuring which meaningful behaviors a specification constrains, without treating proof count or annotation volume as coverage.
status: Mutation-based approaches provide a baseline. A broadly validated semantic coverage measure remains a research target.
why: Helps distinguish substantial verification from superficial assurance.
key_works: Celik et al. (2019), *Mutation Analysis for Coq*; Jain et al. (2020), *mCoq*.

title: Automatic contracts for stateful external APIs
open: Infer candidate contracts for APIs with hidden state, rate limits, retries, and version changes, then validate and maintain explicit assumptions against observations.
status: Deductive tools support contracts, but undocumented external behavior lies outside their proof boundary unless modeled.
why: Makes verification applicable to service-oriented software.
key_works: Why3 project documentation; Newcombe et al. (2015), *How Amazon Web Services Uses Formal Methods*, DOI:10.1145/2699417.

title: Exception-safe functional verification
open: Verify normal results, exceptions, cancellation, cleanup, and partial initialization under one reusable specification discipline for production libraries.
status: Program logics and verified systems address subsets; the target is consistent end-to-end treatment across realistic language and library boundaries.
why: Many operational failures occur on exceptional paths rather than the main algorithm.
key_works: Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*; Gäher et al. (2024), *RefinedRust*, DOI:10.1145/3656422.

title: Modular proof of algorithmic complexity contracts
open: Prove asymptotic and concrete cost contracts that remain valid when clients compose libraries, change data representations, or invoke callbacks.
status: Verified implementations and cost reasoning exist; stable library-level complexity interfaces remain an integration target.
why: Preserves performance guarantees through abstraction.
key_works: CakeML project and publications; Tassarotti, Jung, and Harper (2017), *A Higher-Order Logic for Concurrent Termination-Preserving Refinement*, arXiv:1701.05888.

title: Minimal sufficient annotations without weaker specifications
open: Reduce human annotations while fixing the program semantics and intended specification, with automated checks against weakening preconditions or deleting obligations.
status: LLM-assisted Dafny systems already improve proof automation; specification-preserving annotation reduction remains the relevant target.
why: Reduces verification labor without gaming the task.
key_works: Banerjee, Bouissou, and Zetzsche (2026), *DafnyPro: LLM-Assisted Automated Verification for Dafny Programs*, arXiv:2601.05385.

title: Specification-preserving automated program repair
open: Repair incorrect programs while proving the original specification, preserving required behavior, and bounding unintended changes outside the defect.
status: Specification-guided repair exists in restricted settings. Broad semantic preservation and reliable repair generalization remain open engineering targets.
why: Turns formal specifications into a safe mechanism for automated maintenance.
key_works: Wu, Mendes, and Abreu (2025), *Specification-Guided Repair of Arithmetic Errors in Dafny Programs Using LLMs*, arXiv:2507.03659.

title: Automated liveness proofs for fine-grained concurrent libraries
open: Infer and check termination or progress arguments for substantial lock-free and blocking libraries with minimal manual obligation engineering.
status: TaDA Live establishes compositional reasoning for fine-grained termination; automation at production-library scale is a separate challenge.
why: Goes beyond memory safety and partial correctness to actual progress.
key_works: D’Osualdo, Farzan, Gardner, and Sutherland (2021), *TaDA Live: Compositional Reasoning for Termination of Fine-Grained Concurrent Programs*, arXiv:1901.05750, DOI:10.1145/3477082.

title: Compositional starvation-freedom under realistic schedulers
open: Prove starvation-freedom using scheduler assumptions that can be justified by an actual runtime, including priorities and bounded interference.
status: Fairness-based termination logics exist. Connecting logical fairness assumptions to deployed scheduling policies remains a distinct obligation.
why: Avoids liveness proofs that assume away the operational failure.
key_works: D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*, DOI:10.1145/3477082; Tassarotti et al. (2017), arXiv:1701.05888.

title: Cancellation-safe concurrent protocols
open: Verify that cancellation at every permitted suspension point preserves ownership, releases obligations, and cannot permanently block other participants.
status: Separation logics support sophisticated ownership reasoning; cancellation introduces nonlocal control effects and progress obligations requiring additional treatment.
why: Targets a common failure mode in asynchronous services.
key_works: Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*; D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*.

title: Weak-memory liveness without unjustified fairness transfer
open: Establish reusable conditions under which source-level progress proofs survive compilation to weak-memory hardware.
status: Weak-memory semantics and concurrent termination logics are advanced separately; safety-preserving compilation alone does not establish liveness preservation.
why: Prevents a terminating source proof from masking a hardware-level spin or starvation execution.
key_works: Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics for Relaxed-Memory Concurrency*, DOI:10.1145/3009837.3009850; Tassarotti et al. (2017), arXiv:1701.05888.

title: Verified scalable memory reclamation
open: Verify practical reclamation schemes under weak memory, thread failure, cancellation, and dynamically registered readers, including both safety and reclamation progress.
status: Foundational ownership and weak-memory frameworks exist; the combined operational envelope is the target.
why: Supports safe high-performance concurrent containers without unbounded retired memory.
key_works: Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*; Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics for Relaxed-Memory Concurrency*.

title: Compositional linearizability across foreign-function boundaries
open: Prove linearizability for concurrent components spanning languages, memory models, and calling conventions, with explicit ownership and callback contracts.
status: Language-local logics and source-level concurrency models do not automatically compose across foreign-function interfaces.
why: Matches how real high-performance libraries are assembled.
key_works: Jung et al. (2018), *RustBelt*; Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics for Relaxed-Memory Concurrency*.

title: Crash-and-concurrency liveness
open: Prove that a concurrent service eventually resumes useful work after repeated but suitably bounded crashes, including cleanup of abandoned locks and obligations.
status: Perennial addresses concurrent crash safety; IronFleet and TaDA Live address important liveness settings. Their combined recovery-progress target requires more than safety composition.
why: A service that safely remains stuck is not operationally correct.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Verifying Concurrent, Crash-Safe Systems with Perennial*, DOI:10.1145/3341301.3359632; D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*.

title: Automated refinement between concurrent implementations
open: Automatically prove that an optimized concurrent implementation refines a simpler reference implementation, including observable progress and resource behavior.
status: Higher-order termination-preserving refinement has a logical foundation; large-scale automatic discovery of simulation relations remains a target.
why: Allows aggressive optimization while retaining an understandable specification.
key_works: Tassarotti, Jung, and Harper (2017), *A Higher-Order Logic for Concurrent Termination-Preserving Refinement*, arXiv:1701.05888.

title: Complete mechanized Rust semantic integration
open: Integrate ownership, unsafe code, aliasing, concurrency, panics, and relevant language features into a maintained semantics that supports program proofs and compiler validation.
status: RustBelt, MiniRust, Tree Borrows, and RefinedRust address substantial pieces; this is an integration target, not a claim that Rust lacks formal foundations.
why: Gives different Rust verification tools a coherent semantic reference.
key_works: Jung et al. (2018), *RustBelt*; Jung (2025), *The Current State of MiniRust*; Gäher et al. (2024), *RefinedRust*.

title: Unsafe Rust proofs respecting executable aliasing restrictions
open: Verify substantial unsafe Rust libraries against a precise aliasing model rather than proving functional properties while leaving alias validity outside the argument.
status: Tree Borrows supplies a developed model; 2026 work explicitly advances modular verification against Rust’s pointer-aliasing restrictions.
why: Prevents proofs about executions that the language considers undefined.
key_works: Villani et al. (2025), *Tree Borrows*, DOI:10.1145/3735592; Tas and Jacobs (2026), *Towards Verifying Unsafe Rust Programs against Rust’s Pointer-Aliasing Restrictions*, arXiv:2603.28326.

title: Sound alias-model evolution without ecosystem breakage
open: Develop methods for changing a language’s aliasing model while proving compiler soundness and systematically identifying which previously accepted programs become invalid.
status: Tree Borrows includes substantial empirical and formal evaluation. General migration guarantees across model revisions remain a separate target.
why: Makes semantic improvements compatible with a large existing ecosystem.
key_works: Villani et al. (2025), *Tree Borrows*, DOI:10.1145/3735592; Jung (2023), *From Stacks to Trees*.

title: C provenance semantics aligned across standard, compiler, and verifier
open: Establish a maintained provenance model whose permitted behaviors agree across language specifications, optimizing compilers, and verification tools for a declared C fragment.
status: Cerberus and provenance proposals substantially clarify the problem; complete agreement across the toolchain remains an integration target.
why: Avoids contradictory interpretations of pointer–integer conversions and object identity.
key_works: Memarian et al. (2019), *Exploring C Semantics and Pointer Provenance*; Memarian (2023), *The Cerberus C Semantics*, DOI:10.48456/tr-981.

title: Out-of-thin-air-free semantics with useful global optimizations
open: Reconcile intuitive avoidance of fabricated values with sound aggressive optimization and compositional reasoning for realistic relaxed-memory programs.
status: Promising semantics and Promising 2.0 are major partial solutions. The target concerns coverage, implementation alignment, and reusable verification interfaces, not the absence of candidate semantics.
why: Supports both trustworthy concurrent reasoning and performant compilers.
key_works: Kang et al. (2017), DOI:10.1145/3009837.3009850; Lee et al. (2020), *Promising 2.0: Global Optimizations in Relaxed Memory Concurrency*.

title: Verified async lowering with pinning and cancellation
open: Prove that lowering asynchronous programs into state machines preserves ownership, pinning, cancellation behavior, and observable results.
status: Rust verification foundations and compiler-level models provide components; complete treatment of this combined transformation is the proposed target.
why: Establishes guarantees for a dominant style of systems programming.
key_works: Gäher et al. (2024), *RefinedRust*, DOI:10.1145/3656422; Jung (2025), *The Current State of MiniRust*.

title: Mechanized cross-language undefined-behavior boundaries
open: Specify and prove conditions under which linking components with different undefined-behavior rules preserves each component’s guarantees.
status: C provenance and Rust unsafe-code foundations expose the relevant differences; language-local correctness is insufficient.
why: Supports verified mixed C, Rust, assembly, and managed-language systems.
key_works: Memarian et al. (2019), *Exploring C Semantics and Pointer Provenance*; Jung et al. (2018), *RustBelt*.

title: Empirical conformance testing for formal language semantics
open: Build a maintained corpus that compares formal semantics, interpreters, compiler outputs, and real hardware, with minimized disagreements and adjudicated expected behavior.
status: Tree Borrows and Cerberus demonstrate valuable empirical validation. The target is an ongoing multi-tool semantic observatory.
why: Detects drift between mathematical models and deployed implementations.
key_works: Villani et al. (2025), *Tree Borrows*; Memarian (2023), *The Cerberus C Semantics*, DOI:10.48456/tr-981.

title: Unbounded translation validation for optimizing compiler pipelines
open: Validate meaningful loop and recursion transformations without relying solely on fixed unrolling bounds, and emit independently checkable simulation arguments.
status: Alive2 provides powerful bounded translation validation. Extending coverage to unbounded transformations remains a different problem.
why: Finds or excludes optimization bugs beyond bounded executions.
key_works: Lopes et al. (2021), *Alive2: Bounded Translation Validation for LLVM*, DOI:10.1145/3453483.3454030.

title: Verified optimizing compilation for broader production-language coverage
open: Extend verified compilation to a declared modern language/toolchain envelope, including its concurrency, runtime, exception, and foreign-function features.
status: CompCert and CakeML already demonstrate verified compilers. The open target is broader feature coverage with competitive optimization, not “the first verified compiler.”
why: Reduces the gap between verified source and executable behavior.
key_works: Leroy (2009), *Formal Verification of a Realistic Compiler*; CompCert 3.18 documentation (2026); CakeML project.

title: Verified dynamic linking and plugin loading
open: Preserve component guarantees when loading, replacing, or unloading code at runtime, including symbol resolution, callbacks, and shared-state ownership.
status: Verified compiler and systems projects establish substantial static foundations; dynamic composition adds obligations not implied by a compiler-correctness theorem.
why: Matches plugin-based and hot-updated production systems.
key_works: CompCert project and publications; Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627.

title: Verified JIT deoptimization
open: Prove that speculative optimization, guard failure, stack reconstruction, and deoptimization preserve observable behavior under realistic runtime state.
status: Static compiler correctness and bounded translation validation supply useful techniques; the entire adaptive runtime transition is the target.
why: Addresses correctness risks unique to adaptive execution engines.
key_works: Lopes et al. (2021), *Alive2*, DOI:10.1145/3453483.3454030; Leroy (2009), *Formal Verification of a Realistic Compiler*.

title: Verified GPU compilation across memory hierarchies
open: Prove source-to-device preservation for kernels using shared memory, barriers, atomics, subgroup operations, and host/device transfers.
status: Compiler and ISA semantics address important ingredients; the proposed target combines concurrency semantics with heterogeneous execution.
why: Extends assurance to accelerators used in scientific and AI workloads.
key_works: Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics for ARMv8-A, RISC-V, and CHERI-MIPS*, DOI:10.1145/3290384; Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics*.

title: Semantic preservation of profile-guided optimization
open: Certify optimizations driven by potentially stale or adversarial profiles, proving that profiles affect performance choices but never justify invalid semantic assumptions.
status: Translation validation supplies a promising baseline; profile handling and speculative assumptions must be included in the checked boundary.
why: Allows data-driven optimization without data-driven correctness.

title: Verified garbage collection with concurrent foreign references
open: Prove moving or concurrent garbage collection correct in the presence of foreign pointers, callbacks, safepoints, and weak-memory synchronization.
status: Verified language runtimes demonstrate important collector foundations; cross-language concurrent roots substantially enlarge the proof boundary.
why: Removes a major runtime assumption from high-level program proofs.
key_works: CakeML project, verified runtime and compiler publications; Jung et al. (2018), *Iris from the Ground Up*.

title: Proof-preserving reproducible builds
open: Connect source proofs to reproducible executable artifacts, accounting for build scripts, generated code, linker behavior, tool versions, and dependency selection.
status: Verified compilation proves a semantic relation for a particular pipeline; reproducible-build provenance is an additional end-to-end obligation.
why: Ensures the deployed binary is the binary covered by the proof.
key_works: Leroy (2009), *Formal Verification of a Realistic Compiler*; CakeML project; Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627.

title: End-to-end assurance across kernel hardware assumptions
open: Discharge or explicitly monitor a substantially larger fraction of kernel assumptions about boot code, devices, DMA, and hardware behavior.
status: seL4 has extensive proofs; its AArch64 security proofs were completed in August 2026. The remaining target concerns surrounding assumptions, not that already completed milestone.
why: Extends kernel assurance to the actual deployed platform.
key_works: seL4 Foundation (2026), *Verification* documentation and linked assumptions; Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627.

title: Verified high-performance device drivers
open: Verify production-grade drivers against device models that include interrupts, DMA, reset, timeout, and documented error behavior.
status: Verified-system deployments establish feasibility, but driver/device interfaces remain a major source of assumptions and integration work.
why: Removes privileged components from the unverified perimeter.
key_works: Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627; seL4 verification assumptions.

title: Verified IOMMU and DMA isolation
open: Prove isolation across device assignment, IOMMU configuration, address translation, stale mappings, and device reset.
status: Kernel isolation proofs do not automatically cover unrestricted DMA behavior. The target must include both configuration software and a defensible device model.
why: Prevents peripheral access from invalidating memory-isolation guarantees.
key_works: seL4 Foundation, *Verification* and assumptions documentation; Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics*, DOI:10.1145/3290384.

title: Verified live migration with isolation and continuity
open: Prove that migrating a running virtual machine or sandbox preserves relevant state, isolation, and externally visible execution semantics across failures.
status: Verified kernels and distributed crash reasoning provide foundations; migration joins these domains with device and network state.
why: Enables trustworthy maintenance and load balancing of verified services.

title: Temporal isolation with shared microarchitectural resources
open: Prove useful timing-isolation bounds when components share caches, interconnects, memory controllers, and accelerators.
status: Functional and information-flow kernel proofs do not by themselves establish precise shared-resource timing guarantees.
why: Supports real-time assurance and timing-channel control.
key_works: seL4 verification documentation; Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR*, arXiv:1812.08639.

title: Verified suspend/resume through real platform power transitions
open: Prove state preservation and security across suspend, hibernation, resume, device reinitialization, and interrupted restoration.
status: Kernel and crash-safe-system proofs supply pieces; full platform power transitions cross firmware, device, storage, and kernel boundaries.
why: Extends assurance to normal lifecycle operations rather than only steady-state execution.
key_works: Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627; Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*.

title: Formally verified operational configuration
open: Verify that capabilities, mounts, namespaces, network policy, and startup configuration instantiate the isolation architecture assumed by system proofs.
status: Verified components can still be deployed under incorrect configurations. The target is a checked configuration-to-theorem connection.
why: Prevents operational mistakes from bypassing formal guarantees.
key_works: Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627; seL4 deployment and verification documentation.

title: Low-cost verified platform maintenance
open: Reduce the engineering effort of maintaining a verified kernel-plus-runtime platform across hardware and compiler upgrades by at least 10× on a documented longitudinal baseline.
status: Proposed moonshot; existing deployments demonstrate feasibility but do not establish low ongoing migration cost.
why: Makes verified platforms sustainable beyond a single funded release.
key_works: Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627; Huang et al. (2026), *Lessons from Formally Verified Deployed Software Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3785652.

title: Implementation-level consensus proofs with full operational envelopes
open: Verify a production consensus implementation including serialization, storage, reconfiguration, recovery, and runtime behavior under explicit network assumptions.
status: IronFleet and Grove already verify substantial distributed implementations. The remaining target is broader operational coverage, not basic consensus verification.
why: Closes gaps between an abstract consensus proof and a deployed service.
key_works: Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet*, DOI:10.1145/3068608; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*, arXiv:2309.03046.

title: Rolling-upgrade correctness with mixed protocol versions
open: Prove safety and eventual progress while old and new nodes coexist, including schema changes, rollback, and interrupted deployment.
status: Verified distributed systems provide components; mixed-version operational transitions require explicit compatibility relations.
why: Preserves guarantees during routine deployment.

title: Verified leases with real clock behavior
open: Connect lease safety and liveness proofs to explicit bounds on clock drift, pauses, reboot behavior, and uncertainty in time synchronization.
status: Grove verifies lease-using systems; the proposed extension is a stronger connection to platform clock behavior and operational fault assumptions.
why: Prevents timing assumptions from silently undermining ownership guarantees.
key_works: Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*, arXiv:2309.03046; André (2019), *Parametric Verification*, arXiv:1907.00555.

title: Compositional reconfiguration across multiple services
open: Prove that independently reconfiguring membership, sharding, authorization, and routing preserves global invariants during overlapping transitions.
status: Grove demonstrates verified reconfiguration within substantial systems. Composition of several independently changing control planes is a broader target.
why: Matches modern infrastructure with multiple concurrent controllers.
key_works: Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*, DOI:10.1145/3600006.3613172; Newcombe et al. (2015), *How AWS Uses Formal Methods*.

title: Verified retries across external side-effect boundaries
open: Prove at-most-once or explicitly compensated effects for workflows involving retries and crashes, stating exactly which external systems support idempotency or atomic commit.
status: Crash-safe and distributed proofs supply foundations; unconditional “exactly once” across arbitrary external services is not the target.
why: Prevents duplicated payments, messages, or provisioning actions.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*.

title: Mechanized consistency contracts for client libraries
open: Prove that client-side retries, caches, sessions, and routing preserve the consistency contract exported by a distributed storage service.
status: Server-side proofs and weak-isolation logics provide components; client middleware can introduce behaviors outside a server-only theorem.
why: Makes the guarantee visible to applications match the guarantee actually delivered.
key_works: Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet*; Kaki et al. (2018), *Alone Together*, DOI:10.1145/3158115.

title: Progress proofs under backpressure and overload
open: Prove that bounded queues, admission control, retry policies, and resource pools avoid protocol deadlock and pathological feedback under declared load assumptions.
status: Safety/liveness verification exists for distributed protocols; overload and resource coupling must be included explicitly rather than assumed away.
why: Addresses failures that appear only under operational stress.
key_works: Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet*; D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*.

title: Automatic refinement from design models to service code
open: Maintain a checked relation between high-level protocol models and changing implementation code, including serialization and failure handling.
status: AWS reports substantial benefits from design-level formal methods; implementation-verification systems establish another route. Automatically connecting both remains a valuable target.
why: Prevents model/code drift.
key_works: Newcombe et al. (2015), *How Amazon Web Services Uses Formal Methods*, DOI:10.1145/2699417; Hawblitzel et al. (2017), *IronFleet*.

title: Crash proofs under realistic storage-device behavior
open: Verify recovery while modeling torn writes, reordering, volatile device caches, flush semantics, and documented device failure behavior.
status: Perennial establishes concurrent crash-safe verification. The remaining target is extending and validating the storage model against actual device contracts.
why: Prevents proofs from relying on storage guarantees the hardware does not provide.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Verifying Concurrent, Crash-Safe Systems with Perennial*, DOI:10.1145/3341301.3359632.

title: Verified online compaction and garbage collection
open: Prove that concurrent storage compaction preserves logical contents and recoverability through interruption, crash, and restart, while eventually reclaiming space.
status: Crash-safe concurrent logics provide foundations; the combined safety, recovery, and reclamation-progress target remains workload-specific engineering.
why: Prevents background maintenance from corrupting data or exhausting storage.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; D’Osualdo et al. (2021), *TaDA Live*.

title: End-to-end SQL optimizer equivalence
open: Certify optimization across a declared production SQL fragment including duplicates, NULL behavior, aggregates, ordering where semantically relevant, and supported user-defined functions.
status: Cosette and U-semiring-based work establish substantial equivalence-checking results. Complete production-language coverage remains a broader target.
why: Prevents silent wrong-result query optimizations.
key_works: Chu et al. (2018), *Axiomatic Foundations and Algorithms for Deciding Semantic Equivalences of SQL Queries*, DOI:10.14778/3236187.3236200.

title: Verified query compilation through execution backends
open: Connect relational semantics to executable query plans, code generation, runtime operators, and distributed execution with one compositional proof.
status: Q*cert demonstrates verified query-compilation infrastructure; broad backend and operational coverage remains an extension target.
why: Closes the gap between a correct rewrite and a correct query result.
key_works: Auerbach, Hirzel, Mandel, Shinnar, and Siméon (2017), *Q*cert: A Platform for Implementing and Verifying Query Compilers*; the same authors, *Prototyping a Query Compiler Using Coq*.

title: Implementation proofs of weak isolation
open: Prove that a real database implementation provides its advertised isolation level, including recovery, indexes, replication, and concurrent maintenance.
status: Weak-isolation logics support reasoning about transactions; implementation-level proofs require connecting operational mechanisms to those semantics.
why: Makes advertised consistency guarantees independently checkable.
key_works: Kaki et al. (2018), *Alone Together: Compositional Reasoning and Inference for Weak Isolation*, DOI:10.1145/3158115; *Verifying Isolation Levels of Database Implementations* (2026), arXiv:2607.15877.

title: Minimal synchronization for application invariants
open: Infer the weakest practical isolation or coordination needed to preserve declared application invariants, with checked reasoning about all concurrent transactions.
status: Compositional weak-isolation reasoning and anomaly detection supply partial approaches; optimal coordination choices remain application- and model-dependent.
why: Trades unnecessary synchronization for proved correctness.
key_works: Kaki et al. (2018), *Alone Together*, DOI:10.1145/3158115; *Automated Detection of Serializability Violations under Weak Consistency* (2018), DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2018.41.

title: Verified online schema migration
open: Prove correctness of migrations while reads and writes continue, including mixed application versions, backfills, rollback, and interrupted execution.
status: Query equivalence, crash reasoning, and mixed-version protocols provide ingredients; their integrated migration proof remains the target.
why: Protects data during one of the highest-risk maintenance operations.
key_works: Chu et al. (2018), DOI:10.14778/3236187.3236200; Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*.

title: Verified backup and restore semantics
open: Prove that backups correspond to declared consistency points and that restoration preserves application invariants despite partial uploads, corruption detection, and version changes.
status: Crash-safe and distributed verification establish relevant foundations; backup correctness is not implied by local crash safety.
why: Makes disaster recovery an assured capability rather than an untested assumption.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*.

title: Full processor refinement to executable ISA semantics
open: Prove that a substantial out-of-order processor implementation refines its architectural model across speculation, exceptions, interrupts, and memory ordering.
status: Sail ISA models and parametric hardware-verification frameworks provide major foundations; a full implementation proof remains specific to a processor and feature envelope.
why: Connects software proofs to the hardware executing them.
key_works: Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics for ARMv8-A, RISC-V, and CHERI-MIPS*, DOI:10.1145/3290384; Choi et al. (2017), *Kami*, DOI:10.1145/3110268.

title: Parameterized cache-coherence proofs with implementation detail
open: Verify scalable coherence implementations for arbitrary supported core counts while including realistic buffering, eviction, DMA, and heterogeneous agents.
status: Kami demonstrates parametric hardware verification; richer industrial coherence envelopes remain a distinct target.
why: Avoids relying exclusively on bounded small-core model checking.
key_works: Choi et al. (2017), *Kami: A Platform for High-Level Parametric Hardware Specification and Its Modular Verification*, DOI:10.1145/3110268.

title: Fault-tolerant adaptive network-on-chip verification
open: Prove safety, deadlock freedom, and useful progress for adaptive routing under link/router failures across parameterized topologies.
status: NoC-Out in 2026 verifies a multidimensional torus generator with strong liveness. Adaptive fault-tolerant routing is a narrower extension, not an untouched field.
why: Supports reliable many-core communication fabrics.
key_works: Kurze, Farka, and Ertel (2026), *NoC-Out: A Formally-Verified Network-on-Chip Library for Rule-Based Hardware Designs*, arXiv:2608.24478.

title: Composable hardware/software speculation contracts
open: Develop contracts that let software proofs remain valid across several compliant speculative microarchitectures without modeling every implementation detail.
status: SPECTECTOR and hardware/software-contract research establish substantial partial approaches. Portability and composition across modern features remain targets.
why: Makes speculative-execution security more reusable.
key_works: Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR: Principled Detection of Speculative Information Flows*, arXiv:1812.08639; associated *Hardware/Software Contracts for Secure Speculation* resources.

title: Physical leakage guarantees beyond constant-time timing models
open: Connect RTL-level proofs to explicit power or electromagnetic leakage models and validate where those models accurately bound observable information.
status: Iodine verifies hardware constant-time properties. Constant-time execution does not itself prove absence of power or electromagnetic leakage.
why: Prevents timing proofs from being overinterpreted as complete side-channel security.
key_works: von Gleissenthall et al. (2019), *Iodine: Verifying Constant-Time Execution of Hardware*, arXiv:1910.03111.

title: Verified clock-domain and reset-domain integration
open: Prove digital protocols correct under explicitly modeled asynchronous clock relationships, reset sequencing, and metastability-containment assumptions.
status: Digital hardware frameworks provide logical foundations; analog phenomena must remain explicit assumptions or be connected to validated physical models.
why: Addresses failures that ordinary synchronous RTL reasoning misses.
key_works: Choi et al. (2017), *Kami*, DOI:10.1145/3110268; Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics*, DOI:10.1145/3290384.

title: Proof-preserving hardware optimization and physical-design handoff
open: Maintain checked equivalence from verified hardware descriptions through optimization, synthesis, and implementation transformations under explicit timing assumptions.
status: High-level hardware proofs do not automatically cover every downstream tool transformation.
why: Ensures fabricated designs correspond to verified descriptions.
key_works: Choi et al. (2017), *Kami*, DOI:10.1145/3110268; Kurze et al. (2026), *NoC-Out*, arXiv:2608.24478.

title: Tenfold reduction in hardware proof maintenance cost
open: Achieve a measured 10× reduction in proof-update effort across a realistic sequence of microarchitectural revisions, without reducing properties or supported configurations.
status: Proposed moonshot grounded in modular and parameterized hardware-verification frameworks.
why: Makes formal verification compatible with fast hardware iteration.
key_works: Choi et al. (2017), *Kami*; Kurze et al. (2026), *NoC-Out*.

title: End-to-end verified post-quantum implementation suites
open: Verify a declared post-quantum cryptographic suite from mathematical operations through optimized code, serialization, error handling, and supported deployment platforms.
status: EverCrypt and Fiat Cryptography demonstrate powerful verified-implementation techniques; complete suite coverage must be established algorithm by algorithm.
why: Reduces implementation risk during cryptographic migration.
key_works: Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider*; Erbsen et al. (2019), *Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic—With Proofs, Without Compromises*.

title: Verified vectorized cryptography across architectures
open: Produce high-performance vectorized implementations with proofs that cover instruction semantics, lane operations, alignment, and fallback dispatch.
status: EverCrypt verifies cross-platform cryptographic components and dispatch mechanisms; broad architecture and algorithm coverage remains a continuing target.
why: Prevents assurance from requiring unacceptable performance loss.
key_works: Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*; Armstrong et al. (2019), *ISA Semantics*, DOI:10.1145/3290384.

title: Constant-time preservation through complete compilation
open: Prove that the compilation and linking pipeline preserves a precisely stated leakage property for cryptographic code, not just functional behavior.
status: Verified cryptographic libraries and speculative-flow analyses provide components; ordinary compiler correctness does not imply leakage preservation.
why: Prevents optimizations from reintroducing secrets-dependent behavior.
key_works: Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*; Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR*, arXiv:1812.08639.

title: Verified masked implementations under realistic leakage models
open: Combine correctness and masking-security proofs with concrete assumptions about glitches, transitions, randomness reuse, and compiler transformations.
status: Constant-time and verified arithmetic work supply only part of this assurance; masking requires richer leakage reasoning.
why: Addresses physical leakage that constant-time code alone does not exclude.
key_works: von Gleissenthall et al. (2019), *Iodine*, arXiv:1910.03111; Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*.

title: Verified cryptographic fault defenses
open: Prove that an implementation detects or safely handles a declared class of injected faults, including faults affecting control flow, checks, and outputs.
status: Functional correctness proofs generally assume fault-free execution; hardware and cryptographic verification provide foundations for explicit fault extensions.
