why: Protects high-value cryptographic operations against physical fault attacks.
key_works: Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*; Choi et al. (2017), *Kami*.

title: Proven cryptographic agility without downgrade paths
open: Verify negotiation, algorithm replacement, fallback, and configuration changes so that cryptographic agility cannot silently reduce the required security level.
status: EverCrypt proves important agility mechanisms; whole-protocol negotiation and operational configuration enlarge the target.
why: Makes migration capability compatible with stable security guarantees.
key_works: Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*; Tamarin prover, protocol-analysis documentation and case studies.

title: Verified entropy acquisition and random-number lifecycle
open: Connect probabilistic security proofs to entropy acquisition, seeding, reseeding, state compromise, process cloning, and restart behavior.
status: Mathematical cryptographic proofs and verified implementations frequently expose randomness assumptions; discharging the operational lifecycle is an additional target.
why: Prevents correct algorithms from failing because their randomness assumptions are false.
key_works: Project Everest, project documentation; Protzenko et al. (2020), *EverCrypt*.

title: Automated verified arithmetic generation beyond prime-field kernels
open: Extend synthesis of proved, competitive arithmetic code to broader algebraic structures and operation sequences, including architecture-specific optimization.
status: Fiat Cryptography demonstrates that generated arithmetic can be both proved and fast; broader algebraic and backend coverage remains the target.
why: Reduces hand-written low-level arithmetic and its associated audit burden.
key_works: Erbsen, Philipoom, Gross, Sloan, and Chlipala (2019), *Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic—With Proofs, Without Compromises*.

title: Symbolic-to-computational security with implementation alignment
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Connect symbolic protocol proofs to computational security statements and the actual encoding and cryptographic API behavior of implementations.
status: Tamarin analyzes substantial real protocols; a symbolic proof does not automatically supply every computational and implementation correspondence.
why: Makes protocol assurance meaningful across abstraction layers.
key_works: Tamarin prover, documentation and published TLS, 5G, Noise, EMV, and messaging case studies; Project Everest.

title: Scalable protocol proof under key compromise and recovery
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Verify long-running protocols through repeated compromise, key rotation, device replacement, and recovery, with explicit guarantees for each phase.
status: Modern protocol analyses already cover rich security properties. The combined lifecycle and state-space burden remains a scoped scaling target.
why: Models security over years of operation rather than one clean session.
key_works: Tamarin prover and its modern messaging/security-protocol case studies.

title: Authorization proofs across identity and application boundaries
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Prove that tokens, sessions, delegated credentials, revocation, and application permissions enforce one intended authorization policy across services.
status: Protocol-analysis and verified-system tools provide ingredients; operational identity composition is a separate assurance target.
why: Prevents confused-deputy and stale-authorization failures.
key_works: Tamarin prover documentation; Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627.

title: Noninterference with explicit declassification budgets
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Verify systems that intentionally release selected information while proving that all other flows remain bounded by a precise policy.
status: Hyperproperty and leakage-verification frameworks provide foundations. Practical policy composition and quantitative declassification remain challenging.
why: Replaces unrealistic “release nothing” policies with useful security guarantees.
key_works: *HyperProb* (2021), DOI:10.1007/978-3-030-90870-6_35; Guarnieri et al. (2020), *SPECTECTOR*.

title: Automatic coupling discovery for privacy proofs
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Discover and independently check probabilistic couplings for privacy proofs beyond fixed, hand-designed coupling templates.
status: Coupling-based logics already verify important mechanisms, including analyses not captured by simple composition alone.
why: Reduces specialized mathematical effort in differential-privacy verification.
key_works: Barthe, Gaboardi, Grégoire, Hsu, and Strub (2016), *Proving Differential Privacy via Probabilistic Couplings*, arXiv:1601.05047, DOI:10.1145/2933575.2934554.

title: End-to-end finite-precision differential privacy
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Prove privacy for executable mechanisms including floating-point sampling, clipping, rounding, exceptional values, and observable failures.
status: Mathematical privacy proofs and finite-precision verification exist separately; their end-to-end connection is essential.
why: Prevents ideal-real-number proofs from hiding implementation leakage.
key_works: Barthe et al. (2016), arXiv:1601.05047; Becker et al. (2018), *A Verified Certificate Checker for Finite-Precision Error Bounds*, arXiv:1707.02115.

title: Verified adaptive privacy accounting
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Verify privacy-budget accounting when queries, stopping rules, and mechanisms are chosen adaptively, including persistent state and crash recovery.
status: Relational probabilistic logics establish important privacy foundations. Stateful operational accounting adds software and lifecycle obligations.
why: Prevents a correct mechanism from being overused by an incorrect service.
key_works: Barthe et al. (2016), *Proving Differential Privacy via Probabilistic Couplings*; Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*.

title: Privacy proofs across distributed data pipelines
subfield: Security protocols, information flow, and privacy
open: Compose proofs across ingestion, joins, contribution bounding, private aggregation, caching, and output publication under explicit trust boundaries.
status: Mechanism-level privacy and query-compilation verification provide foundations; pipeline semantics can invalidate mechanism assumptions.
why: Makes privacy guarantees apply to the delivered data product.
key_works: Barthe et al. (2016), arXiv:1601.05047; Auerbach et al. (2017), *Q*cert*.

title: Scalable certified floating-point error analysis with branches
open: Produce tight end-to-end error bounds when rounding can change control flow, including paths near branch boundaries.
status: FloVer verifies numerical error certificates; unstable tests and discrete choices introduce additional analysis challenges.
why: Prevents small arithmetic errors from triggering large behavioral changes.
key_works: Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; Lohar, Darulova, Putot, and Goubault (2018), *Discrete Choice in the Presence of Numerical Uncertainties*.

title: Certified elementary-function implementations across full domains
open: Verify accuracy and exceptional behavior of production elementary functions across all supported inputs, rounding modes, and implementation branches.
status: Dandelion certifies approximations; connecting approximation proofs to complete optimized library implementations remains broader work.
why: Removes a pervasive numerical trusted component.
key_works: *Dandelion: Certified Approximations of Elementary Functions* (2022), arXiv:2202.05472; Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115.

title: Verified mixed-precision optimization
open: Automatically choose precisions and transformations that meet a proved error tolerance while optimizing actual execution cost on a target platform.
status: Finite-precision certificate checking provides a foundation; joint optimization of precision, control flow, and hardware performance remains the target.
why: Improves performance and energy without sacrificing stated numerical accuracy.
key_works: Becker et al. (2018), *A Verified Certificate Checker for Finite-Precision Error Bounds*, DOI:10.23919/FMCAD.2018.8603019.

title: Verified parallel reductions with reproducibility guarantees
open: Prove numerical bounds and reproducibility properties for parallel reductions across changing thread counts, scheduling, and vectorization.
status: Arithmetic verification and concurrency semantics provide components; nonassociative floating-point operations make parallel composition nontrivial.
why: Supports reproducible scientific and machine-learning computation.
key_works: Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; Kang et al. (2017), *A Promising Semantics*.

title: Certified iterative solver termination and accuracy
open: Verify stopping criteria for iterative numerical solvers under roundoff, ill-conditioning, and finite resource limits, including justified failure reports.
status: Certified numerical reasoning exists, but convergence theorems over exact arithmetic do not automatically justify executable stopping tests.
why: Prevents silent acceptance of inaccurate numerical solutions.
key_works: Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; Gao et al., dReal research publications.

title: End-to-end verified scientific simulation pipelines
open: Connect discretization error, numerical error, solver behavior, and implementation correctness for a declared simulation task.
status: Formal numerical and hybrid-system tools address pieces; the full chain must distinguish modeling error from software error.
why: Gives scientific conclusions an explicit computational assurance boundary.

title: Numerical proof transfer to optimized machine code
open: Preserve a proved numerical error bound through compiler transformations, fused operations, vectorization, and library substitution.
status: Verified compilation and numerical certificates are established separately; preserving quantitative error contracts is stronger than ordinary functional refinement.
why: Keeps source-level numerical proofs valid in optimized deployments.

title: Tenfold cheaper certified numerical analysis
open: Reduce certificate-generation-plus-checking cost by at least 10× on a fixed suite while preserving error bounds and coverage of exceptional behavior.
status: Proposed moonshot using FloVer, Dandelion, and related numerical tools as explicit baselines.
why: Makes numerical assurance affordable in routine scientific development.
key_works: Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; *Dandelion* (2022), arXiv:2202.05472.

title: Automatic discovery of nonlinear differential invariants
open: Automatically discover useful invariants for nonlinear dynamics and produce independently checked proofs, including difficult parameterized systems.
status: Differential dynamic logic and KeYmaera X provide a mature proof foundation; invariant discovery remains a major automation burden.
why: Reduces manual mathematical work in hybrid safety proofs.
key_works: Platzer (2016), *A Complete Uniform Substitution Calculus for Differential Dynamic Logic*, DOI:10.1007/s10817-016-9385-1; Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*.

title: Verified sampled-data implementation of continuous controllers
open: Prove that a sampled implementation preserves a continuous controller’s guarantees under finite precision, execution delay, and bounded scheduling jitter.
status: Hybrid-system reasoning and numerical verification provide components; ideal continuous proofs alone do not establish implementation safety.
why: Bridges controller mathematics and embedded execution.
key_works: Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*; Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115.

title: Compositional safety for interacting hybrid components
open: Derive local contracts whose composition proves global safety despite feedback, shared resources, and coupled continuous dynamics.
status: Hybrid proof systems are expressive; useful automatic contract discovery and scalable composition remain separate targets.
why: Avoids monolithic proofs for complex cyber-physical systems.
key_works: Platzer (2016), DOI:10.1007/s10817-016-9385-1; Mitsch and Platzer (2017), *The KeYmaera X Proof IDE*, arXiv:1701.08469.

title: Formal treatment of contact, impacts, and mode explosion
open: Verify robotic or mechanical systems with contact changes, impacts, and friction under explicit physical abstractions, while controlling combinatorial growth in modes.
status: Hybrid verification provides a framework, but realistic contact dynamics and model uncertainty create additional difficulties.
why: Extends formal guarantees to manipulation and locomotion.
key_works: Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*; Gao et al., dReal and satisfiability-modulo-ODE publications.

title: Verified prevention of Zeno behavior in synthesized controllers
open: Synthesize or repair hybrid controllers with proofs excluding infinitely many discrete transitions in finite time while retaining their safety objectives.
status: Hybrid logics can express relevant reasoning; automatic construction of useful non-Zeno guarantees remains a specific target.
why: Ensures mathematical controllers correspond to physically executable behavior.
key_works: Platzer (2016), DOI:10.1007/s10817-016-9385-1; KeYmaera X documentation.

title: Safe learning of dynamics with explicit model-validity regions
open: Learn dynamics and simultaneously maintain certified regions where the learned model’s error bounds justify controller guarantees.
status: Verified-AI and hybrid verification research identify model uncertainty as central; sampled prediction accuracy is not a safety certificate.
why: Makes learning-based control compatible with defensible guarantees.
key_works: Seshia, Sadigh, and Sastry (2022), *Towards Verified Artificial Intelligence*, arXiv:1606.08514.

title: Verifiable recovery controllers under actuator degradation
open: Prove safe fallback behavior when sensors or actuators degrade within explicitly modeled failure sets, including detection delay and switching behavior.
status: Hybrid proof tools support safety reasoning; combined diagnosis, degraded dynamics, and implementation timing form the proposed target.
why: Preserves safety when normal-controller assumptions stop holding.
key_works: KeYmaera X publications; Sánchez et al. (2019), *A Survey of Challenges for Runtime Verification from Advanced Application Domains*, arXiv:1811.06740.

title: Proof-producing high-dimensional reachability
open: Scale conservative reachability analysis to high-dimensional nonlinear systems while exporting certificates checked independently of the numerical reachability engine.
status: δ-complete solvers and hybrid theorem provers provide complementary baselines; dimension and nonlinearity remain substantial scaling barriers.
why: Makes large cyber-physical safety analyses independently auditable.
key_works: Gao et al., dReal publications; Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*.

title: Sound monitoring with missing and reordered events
open: Give monitors explicit semantics for dropped, duplicated, delayed, and reordered observations, returning justified uncertainty rather than false certainty.
status: Distributed and advanced-domain runtime verification recognizes observation quality as a core challenge.
why: Makes monitoring guarantees robust to real telemetry pipelines.
key_works: Sánchez et al. (2019), *A Survey of Challenges for Runtime Verification from Advanced Application Domains*, DOI:10.1007/s10703-019-00337-w, arXiv:1811.06740.

title: Verified instrumentation with bounded observer effects
open: Prove that instrumentation captures the required events while preserving relevant behavior and respecting explicit timing and resource budgets.
status: Runtime monitoring depends on an observation mechanism; its correctness and perturbation cost are separate from the monitor’s logical correctness.
why: Prevents the monitoring system from invalidating the assumptions being monitored.
key_works: Sánchez et al. (2019), arXiv:1811.06740; Ringer et al. (2020), *REPLICA: REPL Instrumentation for Coq Analysis*.

title: Distributed monitoring with optimal communication
open: Determine and approach communication lower bounds for monitoring selected temporal properties under explicit clock and failure models.
status: Distributed runtime verification is established; tight property-dependent communication trade-offs remain a useful theory frontier.
why: Makes monitoring feasible on constrained networks.

title: Minimal-intervention enforcement with hard deadlines
open: Synthesize enforcers that satisfy a temporal policy while minimizing modifications and proving that intervention itself meets deadlines.
status: Timed runtime enforcement is established, including time-retardant constructions. Hard real-time minimal intervention is a stricter target.
why: Avoids enforcing safety by making the system unusable.
key_works: Pinisetty et al. (2012), *Runtime Enforcement of Timed Properties*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-35632-2_23; *Runtime Enforcement of CPS against Signal Temporal Logic* (2025), DOI:10.1145/3716863.3718052.

title: Runtime enforcement of relational properties
open: Enforce useful hyperproperties across multiple executions or users without retaining unbounded histories or unjustifiably restricting benign behavior.
status: Gray-box hyperproperty enforcement is an active research direction; ordinary single-trace safety monitoring does not settle it.
why: Supports runtime enforcement of information-flow and cross-session policies.
key_works: Hsu et al. (2025), *Gray-Box Runtime Enforcement of Hyperproperties*, Acta Informatica paper.

title: Correct monitor evolution during live operation
open: Update policies and monitor implementations while preserving the meaning of accumulated state and avoiding gaps or duplicate enforcement.
status: Stateful monitors and proof-maintenance techniques provide ingredients; live semantic migration is an additional target.
why: Allows policies to evolve without temporarily losing assurance.
key_works: Pinisetty et al. (2012), *Runtime Enforcement of Timed Properties*; Palmskog et al. (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*.

title: Runtime verification of inferred vehicle behavior
open: Validate that inferred behavioral models cover relevant legitimate modes and detect meaningful attacks without conflating unseen benign behavior with violations.
status: Desai et al. demonstrate stateful inference and enforcement for vehicle networks in 2025; stronger coverage and generalization guarantees remain targets.
why: Connects formal monitoring to systems whose behavior is only partially documented.
key_works: Desai et al. (2025), *Stateful Behavior Inference and Runtime Enforcement for Vehicle Network Security*, USENIX VehicleSec.

title: Proof-carrying runtime monitors
open: Generate executable monitors together with proofs of semantic correctness, instrumentation assumptions, memory bounds, and worst-case execution cost.
status: Monitor synthesis, timed enforcement, and verified compilation supply components; packaging the complete assurance chain is the target.
why: Makes monitoring suitable for systems that cannot trust a large unchecked enforcement stack.
key_works: Pinisetty et al. (2012), DOI:10.1007/978-3-642-35632-2_23; CakeML project.

title: Complete verification of large transformer components
open: Verify declared properties of transformer blocks with attention, normalization, nonlinearities, and realistic numerical semantics at substantially larger scales.
status: Neural verification competitions demonstrate progress on diverse models; architectural and scale coverage remain central frontiers.
why: Extends assurance beyond small or specially structured networks.
key_works: Kaulen et al. (2025), *The 6th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition: Summary and Results*, arXiv:2512.19007; VNN-COMP 2026 resources.

title: Deployment-faithful neural-network certificates
open: Prove that a certificate applies to the deployed quantized and optimized executable, including kernels, rounding, graph rewrites, and preprocessing.
status: Network-level verification and numerical/compiler verification provide separate pieces; a mathematical network certificate does not automatically cover its deployment pipeline.
why: Prevents proof/model mismatch.
key_works: Kaulen et al. (2025), arXiv:2512.19007; Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115; Lopes et al. (2021), *Alive2*.

title: Semantic perturbation specifications
open: Define and validate perturbation sets corresponding to meaningful real-world changes rather than relying exclusively on convenient numerical norm balls.
status: Verified-AI research identifies specification and environment modeling as central. Better solvers cannot compensate for irrelevant property definitions.
why: Makes robustness certificates useful outside benchmark abstractions.
key_works: Seshia, Sadigh, and Sastry (2022), *Towards Verified Artificial Intelligence*, arXiv:1606.08514.

title: Relational verification of learned models
open: Scale verification of properties comparing outputs across inputs, groups, model versions, or execution conditions, with precise quantifiers and deployment semantics.
status: Relational and hyperproperty benchmark efforts already exist; the target is broader coverage and scalable certified solving, not the first such benchmark.
why: Supports consistency, fairness, and model-update guarantees.
key_works: VNN-COMP 2025 relational benchmark discussions; *HyperProb* (2021); Kaulen et al. (2025), arXiv:2512.19007.

title: Closed-loop verification with neural perception
open: Prove system-level safety when a neural perception component feeds a controller, including uncertainty, timing, and temporal correlation in perception errors.
status: Neural and hybrid verification each provide methods; isolated network robustness does not imply closed-loop safety.
why: Targets actual autonomous-system behavior.
key_works: Seshia et al. (2022), arXiv:1606.08514; Fulton et al. (2015), *KeYmaera X*.

title: Certified robustness under model updates
open: Transfer or repair guarantees after fine-tuning, pruning, quantization, or architecture changes, proving exactly which input regions and properties remain covered.
status: Existing verification tools provide one-model baselines; efficient longitudinal certificate reuse is a distinct target.
why: Makes verification compatible with continuously updated models.
key_works: Kaulen et al. (2025), arXiv:2512.19007; Palmskog et al. (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*.

title: Independently checkable neural verification certificates
open: Standardize compact certificates for neural verification results across solver families, including numerical soundness and preprocessing provenance.
status: VNN-COMP offers shared evaluation infrastructure; independent certificate interoperability is an additional assurance objective.
why: Avoids trusting every numerical and optimization component of a large verifier.
key_works: Brix et al. (2023), *First Three Years of the International Verification of Neural Networks Competition*, DOI:10.1007/s10009-023-00703-4; Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115.

title: Hundredfold cheaper neural verification at fixed guarantees
open: Achieve a 100× reduction in total compute or energy on a frozen realistic benchmark family without weakening properties, changing numerical semantics, or excluding hard instances.
status: Proposed moonshot; competition results supply baselines, but comparisons must include preprocessing and certificate checking.
why: Makes verification plausible during model development rather than only after deployment.
key_works: Kaulen et al. (2025), arXiv:2512.19007; VNN-COMP 2026 resources.

title: Complete mediation of agent side effects
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Prove that every externally visible agent action passes through a policy-enforcing boundary, including subprocesses, delegated agents, plugins, and direct network access.
status: AgentSpec demonstrates customizable runtime enforcement; complete mediation across a realistic execution environment remains a stronger target.
why: Makes safety independent of whether the language model follows instructions.
key_works: Wang, Poskitt, and Sun (2025), *AgentSpec: Customizable Runtime Enforcement for Safe and Reliable LLM Agents*, arXiv:2503.18666.

title: Formal authority boundaries for delegated agents
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Specify and prove how permissions, data access, budgets, and approval requirements propagate through delegation without accidental privilege amplification.
status: Runtime policy systems provide a baseline; multi-agent authority composition needs explicit semantics.
why: Prevents delegated work from bypassing the original user’s constraints.
key_works: Wang et al. (2025), *AgentSpec*, arXiv:2503.18666; Tamarin prover, authorization-protocol modeling facilities.

title: Crash-safe agent action ledgers
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Prove that an agent’s retained action state, approvals, retries, and tool outcomes preserve the declared side-effect semantics across crashes and continuation.
status: Crash-safe systems and distributed logics provide suitable foundations; applying them to nondeterministic agent workflows requires an explicit action protocol.
why: Prevents duplicate or unauthorized actions after interruption.
key_works: Chajed et al. (2019), *Perennial*; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*; Wang et al. (2025), *AgentSpec*.

title: Formal prompt-injection containment at tool boundaries
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Prove a bounded security property such as “untrusted retrieved text cannot authorize new privileges or external recipients,” without claiming universal semantic immunity to prompt injection.
status: Policy enforcement supplies a practical route; guarantees must be stated over observable authority and actions rather than undefined notions of model obedience.
why: Converts a vague behavioral goal into enforceable system invariants.
key_works: Wang et al. (2025), *AgentSpec*, arXiv:2503.18666; Seshia et al. (2022), arXiv:1606.08514.

title: Proof-generating agents that cannot alter the task
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Ensure automated verifiers and coding agents cannot improve their score by weakening specifications, deleting assertions, introducing trusted axioms, or changing the checked artifact.
status: DafnyPro explicitly uses checks against unauthorized changes; broader cross-tool enforcement remains a target.
why: Makes proof success evidence about the requested program rather than a modified problem.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2026), *DafnyPro*, arXiv:2601.05385; Loughridge et al. (2024), *DafnyBench*, arXiv:2406.08467.

title: Repository-scale verified code generation
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Generate and maintain verified changes across existing repositories with dependencies, interfaces, concurrency, and realistic build constraints, not just isolated functions.
status: DafnyBench and 2026 agentic Dafny systems show substantial bounded-task progress. Repository-scale maintenance remains a different evaluation target.
why: Connects formal code generation to useful software development.
key_works: Loughridge et al. (2024), *DafnyBench*, arXiv:2406.08467; Breen et al. (2026), *AxDafny: Agentic Verified Code Generation in Dafny*, arXiv:2606.32007.

title: Verified functional correctness plus practical performance
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Have code-generation agents satisfy the original specification and explicit asymptotic or concrete performance constraints, with checked evidence for both.
status: AxDafny distinguishes proof success from runtime performance; high verification scores alone do not establish efficient implementations.
why: Avoids formally correct but unusably slow generated software.
key_works: Breen et al. (2026), *AxDafny*, arXiv:2606.32007.

title: Contamination-resistant longitudinal agent-verification benchmarks
subfield: LLM agents and learned verification systems
open: Build versioned benchmarks with held-out future changes, hidden specifications, dependency constraints, and complete artifact provenance to measure durable verification ability.
status: DafnyBench provides an important dataset; static benchmark success does not measure resistance to contamination or maintenance drift.
why: Separates genuine verification capability from memorization and benchmark-specific behavior.
key_works: Loughridge et al. (2024), *DafnyBench*, arXiv:2406.08467; Banerjee et al. (2026), *DafnyPro*, arXiv:2601.05385.

title: Complete machine-checked metatheory for Lean’s implemented kernel
open: Complete the correctness argument connecting Lean’s implemented type checker to an explicit formal account of its logic and conversion behavior.
status: Lean4Lean has an executable checker and proofs of important parts; the July 2026 publication still describes remaining formalization work.
why: Reduces reliance on informal arguments about a widely used proof kernel.
key_works: Carneiro (2024), *Lean4Lean: Towards a Verified Typechecker for Lean, in Lean*, arXiv:2403.14064; Carneiro (2026), DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.TYPES.2025.2.

title: Verified kernel implementation through executable artifacts
open: Connect a proved type-checking algorithm to the actual executable checker, covering compilation, runtime, parsing, and serialization.
status: MetaRocq, Lean4Lean, and verified language implementations address different parts of this chain; algorithm correctness alone does not discharge all executable assumptions.
why: Makes proof checking trustworthy at the artifact actually run.
key_works: Sozeau et al. (2020), *Coq Coq Correct!*, DOI:10.1145/3371076; Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*; CakeML project.

title: Cross-assistant proof transfer with explicit logical assumptions
open: Transfer substantial proofs between assistants while recording differences in axioms, universes, equality, and computation, and checking every translation step.
status: Dedukti and logical-framework work provide important interoperability mechanisms; broad semantics-preserving transfer remains a continuing target.
why: Avoids duplicating expensive formal developments and exposes hidden assumptions.
key_works: Assaf et al., *Dedukti: A Logical Framework Based on the λΠ-Calculus Modulo Theory*; Cauderlier and Halmagrand (2015), *Checking Zenon Modulo Proofs in Dedukti*, arXiv:1507.08719.

title: Safe extensible computation inside proof checking
open: Support efficient domain-specific computation in proof assistants without admitting unsound external evaluators or opaque trusted plugins.
status: Reflection, extraction, and certified checking provide routes; preserving extensibility while keeping a small trusted boundary remains the target.
why: Makes large computational proofs practical without sacrificing assurance.
key_works: Sozeau et al. (2020), *Coq Coq Correct!*; Tan et al. (2021), *cake_lpr*; Becker et al. (2018), arXiv:1707.02115.

title: Verified extraction across effects and foreign interfaces
open: Prove extraction correct for programs that use realistic effects, external libraries, and language-specific representations, including the assumptions of the target runtime.
status: MetaRocq verifies substantial type-checking and erasure foundations; extensions to Rust and Elm demonstrate additional directions.
why: Makes executable programs inherit the intended meaning of their source proofs.
key_works: Sozeau et al. (2020), DOI:10.1145/3371076; Annenkov, Milo, Nielsen, and Spitters (2021), *Extending MetaCoq Erasure: Extraction to Rust and Elm*.

title: Adversarially robust proof checking
open: Make proof checkers resistant to maliciously expensive terms, parser attacks, resource exhaustion, and corrupted proof artifacts without rejecting valid ordinary workloads unnecessarily.
status: Small logical kernels address logical soundness, not automatically implementation security or denial-of-service resistance.
why: Enables proof checking as an exposed service or supply-chain gate.
key_works: Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*; Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*.

title: Proof-preserving parallel and distributed kernel checking
open: Parallelize checking with verified dependency partitioning, deterministic acceptance, and sound recovery from worker failure.
status: Parallel regression proving exists; foundationally justified distributed checking and operational recovery are stronger requirements.
why: Scales proof validation without centralizing trust in an unchecked scheduler.
key_works: Palmskog, Celik, and Gligoric (2018), *piCoq: Parallel Regression Proving for Large-Scale Verification Projects*; Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*.

title: Formal assumption accounting for complete developments
open: Produce machine-readable reports of every axiom, admitted theorem, unsafe extension, extraction assumption, and external trust dependency used by a delivered artifact.
status: Proof assistants expose portions of this information; the target is a complete cross-tool, artifact-level account.
why: Makes “formally verified” a precise, inspectable claim.
key_works: MetaRocq project documentation; Dedukti framework publications; Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*, DOI:10.1561/2500000045.

title: Proof repair across semantic data-representation changes
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Repair proofs after changing data representations while preserving theorem meaning through an explicit equivalence or refinement map.
status: Ornaments and proof-reuse tools demonstrate meaningful automation; large heterogeneous developments remain challenging.
why: Allows verified software to evolve beyond superficial edits.
key_works: Ringer, Yazdani, Leo, and Grossman (2019), *Ornaments for Proof Reuse in Coq*; the same authors (2018), *Adapting Proof Automation to Adapt Proofs*.

title: Reliable proof migration between assistant versions
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Automate migration across changes in libraries, elaboration, tactics, and kernel interfaces while checking that theorem statements retain their intended meaning.
status: Proof brittleness and maintenance are documented; successful recompilation alone does not establish semantic equivalence of revised statements.
why: Prevents verified developments from becoming frozen on obsolete toolchains.

title: Semantic dependency tracking for proof reuse
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Track enough semantic dependency information to reuse proofs safely after changes while avoiding unnecessary rechecking of unrelated developments.
status: iCoq, piCoq, and machine-checked change-impact analysis establish important baselines.
why: Reduces verification latency in large projects.
key_works: Celik, Palmskog, and Gligoric (2017), *iCoq: Regression Proof Selection for Large-Scale Verification Projects*; Palmskog et al. (2020), *Practical Machine-Checked Formalization of Change Impact Analysis*.

title: Searchable proof libraries across incompatible vocabularies
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Retrieve and adapt relevant lemmas across libraries that encode the same mathematics or program property using different representations and naming conventions.
status: Learning-based naming, retrieval, and theorem-proving systems provide partial progress; representation-aware reuse remains harder than text similarity.
why: Reduces rediscovery and duplicated formalization.
key_works: Nie et al. (2020), *Deep Generation of Coq Lemma Names Using Elaborated Terms*; Shen et al. (2025), *REAL-Prover*, arXiv:2505.20613.

title: Human-useful explanations of failed proof search
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Produce faithful explanations identifying missing lemmas, incompatible assumptions, or unsuitable induction principles, validated against actual search behavior.
status: Instrumentation and proof-analysis tools expose traces; turning them into useful, nonfabricated explanations remains a target.
why: Makes automation collaborative rather than opaque.
key_works: Ringer et al. (2020), *REPLICA: REPL Instrumentation for Coq Analysis*; Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*.

title: Automated theorem proving beyond familiar benchmark distributions
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Demonstrate robust proof discovery on genuinely new theories, unfamiliar libraries, and long dependency chains, with all proofs kernel-checked.
status: Modern learned provers achieve substantial benchmark progress; generalization beyond familiar theorem distributions remains a distinct research problem.
why: Determines whether learned proving can support new verification projects.
key_works: Shen et al. (2025), *REAL-Prover*, arXiv:2505.20613; DeepSeek-AI (2025), *DeepSeek-Prover-V2*, project and research resources.

title: Proof minimization without destroying maintainability
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Optimize generated proofs jointly for checking cost, size, readability, and resistance to future library changes.
status: Proof engineering identifies competing concerns; the shortest term or fastest current tactic script need not be the easiest proof to maintain.
why: Prevents automated proving from generating an unmanageable maintenance burden.
key_works: Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*; Ringer et al. (2018), *Adapting Proof Automation to Adapt Proofs*.

title: Tenfold lower human effort for verified maintenance
subfield: Proof engineering, reuse, and automated theorem proving
open: Reduce total human effort by at least 10× across realistic verified-software maintenance tasks while keeping specifications, supported behavior, and trust assumptions fixed.
status: Proposed moonshot. Annotation counts and isolated theorem success are insufficient substitutes for longitudinal effort measurement.
why: Makes formal verification economically sustainable for ordinary development.
key_works: Ringer et al. (2019), *QED at Large*; Huang et al. (2026), *Lessons from Formally Verified Deployed Software Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3785652.

title: Scalable verification of hybrid quantum-classical programs
open: Automatically verify substantial programs combining quantum operations, classical control, arrays, loops, and measurement-dependent behavior.
status: Quantum Hoare logics with classical variables already exist, including relative-completeness results. Scaling automation is the open target.
why: Matches practical quantum software rather than isolated circuits.
key_works: Feng and Ying (2021), *Quantum Hoare Logic with Classical Variables*, arXiv:2008.06812, DOI:10.1145/3456877; Ying (2024), arXiv:2412.09869.

title: Verified quantum optimization under realistic hardware constraints
open: Prove correctness of optimization and mapping while accounting for connectivity, native gates, ancilla management, and measurement-driven control.
status: VOQC already provides verified circuit optimization. Broader hardware-aware adaptive compilation remains an extension target.
why: Preserves algorithm meaning through aggressive quantum compilation.
key_works: Hietala et al. (2021), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, DOI:10.1145/3434318; extended TOPLAS version (2023).

title: Certified approximation budgets for quantum transformations
open: Compose approximation errors from gate synthesis, circuit rewriting, and numerical representation into a checked end-to-end behavioral bound.
status: Exact circuit verification and verified optimizers provide a foundation; approximate transformations require quantitative semantics.
why: Allows useful approximate optimization without losing track of total error.
key_works: Hietala et al. (2021/2023), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*; Paykin, Rand, and Zdancewic (2017), *QWIRE*, DOI:10.1145/3009837.3009894.

title: Noise-model-aware quantum correctness
open: Verify claims about noisy implementations under explicit channel models while separating proved consequences from experimentally estimated noise assumptions.
status: Quantum-program logics establish semantic foundations; operational noise characterization must be connected rather than presumed.
why: Makes formal guarantees meaningful for imperfect hardware.
key_works: Ying (2012), *Floyd–Hoare Logic for Quantum Programs*, DOI:10.1145/2049706.2049708; Feng and Ying (2021), DOI:10.1145/3456877.

title: Verified quantum error-correction controllers
open: Prove the correctness of syndrome processing, decoding interfaces, feed-forward control, and fault handling under an explicit fault model.
status: Circuit and hybrid quantum-classical verification provide components; complete operational error-correction stacks add classical timing and reliability obligations.
why: Supports fault-tolerant quantum computation as a system.
key_works: Feng and Ying (2021), *Quantum Hoare Logic with Classical Variables*; Hietala et al. (2023), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*.

title: Automated quantum loop invariants
open: Discover compact invariants for quantum loops and check them without expanding exponentially large state matrices whenever structure permits.
status: Quantum Hoare logic is established; 2025 work investigates automata-based automation to address representation and scaling.
why: Makes verification of iterative quantum algorithms more practical.
key_works: *Automating Quantum Hoare Logic with Automata* (2025), Workshop on Quantum Software; Ying (2012), DOI:10.1145/2049706.2049708.

title: Verified quantum-language interoperability
open: Prove semantics-preserving translation between circuit languages, hybrid programming languages, and hardware execution formats, including measurement and classical state.
status: QWIRE and verified quantum compilers supply important local foundations; cross-tool semantic alignment remains a broader target.
why: Prevents correctness gaps between independently developed quantum tools.
key_works: Paykin, Rand, and Zdancewic (2017), *QWIRE*; Hietala et al. (2021/2023), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*.

title: Quantum-verification benchmarks with known proof obligations
open: Build a versioned benchmark corpus of realistic quantum programs, transformations, seeded faults, and independently checked expected properties.
status: Quantum frameworks publish examples and artifacts; the proposed target is a shared, longitudinal benchmark with explicit semantic and noise assumptions.
why: Makes progress comparable across proof approaches.
key_works: QWIRE project publications; VOQC project and extended optimizer paper; Liu et al. (2019), *Formal Verification of Quantum Algorithms Using Quantum Hoare Logic*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-030-25543-5_12.

title: Smart-contract proofs preserved across upgrades
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Prove that contract upgrades preserve designated invariants while handling storage-layout changes, authorization, rollback, and mixed-version interactions.
status: ConCert and deployed contract-verification tools establish substantial foundations; upgrade lifecycle correctness is a distinct target.
why: Protects persistent assets and state during software evolution.
key_works: Annenkov, Nielsen, and Spitters (2020), *ConCert: A Smart Contract Certification Framework in Coq*, arXiv:1907.10674; *Translation Certification for Smart Contracts* (2022), arXiv:2201.04919.

title: Cross-contract compositional economic invariants
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Verify system-wide conservation, solvency, and access invariants across interacting contracts under explicit assumptions about external protocols and price inputs.
status: Individual-contract functional verification does not establish arbitrary compositional or economic safety.
why: Targets failures emerging from interactions rather than local coding mistakes.
key_works: Annenkov et al. (2020), *ConCert*, arXiv:1907.10674; KEVM, *A Complete Formal Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine* (2018).

title: Contract guarantees under transaction reordering and censorship
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Prove application properties under explicitly modeled adversarial ordering, delayed inclusion, and bounded or unbounded censorship assumptions.
status: Executable blockchain semantics support operational reasoning; economic and liveness claims require an explicit transaction-scheduling model.
why: Prevents local proofs from assuming a favorable transaction order.
key_works: KEVM (2018), *A Complete Formal Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine*; ConCert, arXiv:1907.10674.

title: Verified cross-chain bridge implementations
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Verify the complete bridge path, including source finality assumptions, message authentication, replay protection, validator changes, and destination execution.
status: Contract semantics and security-protocol tools provide components; a bridge theorem must expose the assumptions of both chains and any external signers.
why: Addresses systems whose risk lies primarily at trust boundaries.
key_works: KEVM project; ConCert; Tamarin prover documentation.

title: Complete mechanized WebAssembly SIMD semantics
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Replace externally delegated or opaque SIMD behavior with explicit mechanized semantics and proofs covering the supported instructions and numerical details.
status: The current WasmCert-Rocq repository formalizes WebAssembly 2.0 plus additions, but describes SIMD execution through reference-implementation functions and opaque opcodes.
why: Closes a concrete semantic coverage gap for performance-critical WebAssembly.
key_works: Bodin, Gardner, Pichon, Watt, and Rao, *WasmCert-Coq/Rocq* project, 2019–2026; Watt (2018), *Mechanising and Verifying the WebAssembly Specification*.

title: Verified WebAssembly host and component boundaries
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Prove security and functional contracts across WebAssembly modules, host imports, resource handles, callbacks, and component-level linking.
status: WasmCert includes type-safety and interpreter-related results; core-language soundness does not automatically verify arbitrary host APIs.
why: Makes sandbox guarantees meaningful for real applications.
key_works: WasmCert-Rocq and WasmCert-Isabelle projects; Iris-Wasm-related program-logic resources linked by WasmCert.

title: Cross-layer verification of API serialization
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Prove that schemas, parsers, serializers, client types, and server handlers agree on values, errors, optional fields, and version compatibility.
status: Verified query and language frameworks provide techniques; API contracts frequently span several independently generated artifacts.
why: Prevents semantic mismatches that evade component-local type checking.
key_works: Díaz et al. (2020), *A Mechanized Formalization of GraphQL*, HAL:hal-02422532; Auerbach et al. (2017), *Q*cert*.

title: Verified application behavior across client, server, and database
subfield: Smart contracts, WebAssembly, and multi-language applications
open: Establish an end-to-end refinement from user-visible operations to client code, service logic, and persistent transactions, including retries and partial failure.
status: GraphQL formalization, query verification, and distributed-system proofs each cover portions; their integrated application-level guarantee remains the target.
why: Makes assurance apply to the behavior users actually observe.
key_works: Díaz et al. (2020), *A Mechanized Formalization of GraphQL*; Kaki et al. (2018), *Alone Together*; Sharma et al. (2023), *Grove*.

title: Causal measurement of formal verification’s defect-reduction effect
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Conduct preregistered, adequately powered studies comparing matched development approaches while measuring escaped defects, severity, labor, and maintenance.
status: Industrial deployments and surveys demonstrate feasibility and report benefits; they do not by themselves identify a general causal effect.
why: Guides where verification produces the greatest practical value.
key_works: Huang et al. (2026), *Lessons from Formally Verified Deployed Software Systems*, DOI:10.1145/3785652; Newcombe et al. (2015), DOI:10.1145/2699417.

title: Longitudinal total-cost dataset for verified software
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Collect multi-year records of specification work, proof construction, onboarding, tool migration, defect repair, and operational maintenance with comparable accounting.
status: Case studies and surveys contain valuable observations; the proposed dataset must capture full lifecycle costs rather than initial proof effort alone.
why: Enables realistic budgeting and comparison of verification approaches.
key_works: Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652; Klein et al. (2018), *Formally Verified Software in the Real World*, DOI:10.1145/3230627.

title: Dataset of failures outside formal proof boundaries
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Build an adjudicated corpus of incidents involving verified components, classifying whether failures arose from specifications, assumptions, integration, deployment, or proof-tool defects.
status: Existing deployed-system reviews identify assurance boundaries; a structured incident corpus would support more precise risk analysis.
why: Reveals where additional verification would actually prevent failures.
key_works: Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652; seL4 verification assumptions documentation.

title: Cross-tool semantic benchmark registry
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Maintain benchmark identities with exact semantics, versions, expected results, certificates, licensing, and known reductions between equivalent instances.
status: SYNTCOMP, VNN-COMP, DafnyBench, and JANI provide important domain-specific infrastructure. The target is interoperability, not replacing those projects.
why: Prevents misleading comparisons caused by different semantics or silently modified tasks.
key_works: SYNTCOMP; VNN-COMP; Loughridge et al. (2024), *DafnyBench*; Budde et al. (2017), *JANI: Quantitative Model and Tool Interaction*.

title: Sustainable funding for proof-kernel and semantics maintenance
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Design and evaluate multi-year funding mechanisms that pay for maintenance, independent review, compatibility work, and incident response rather than only new research features.
status: Proposed funding-design problem, not a claim that these projects receive no funding. Maintained kernels and semantics are continuing dependencies of high-assurance systems.
why: Prevents critical assurance infrastructure from depending on intermittent project grants.
key_works: Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.TYPES.2025.2; MetaRocq project; Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627.

title: Shared access to realistic industrial verification benchmarks
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Establish governance and funding that permit release or safe hosted evaluation of realistic industrial instances while protecting legitimate confidentiality.
status: Public competitions and industrial case studies show complementary strengths; confidentiality can prevent realistic workloads from becoming reusable research assets.
why: Reduces the gap between academic benchmarks and operational difficulty.
key_works: Newcombe et al. (2015), *How AWS Uses Formal Methods*; Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652; SYNTCOMP and VNN-COMP resources.

title: Reusable assurance evidence across procurement and certification
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Develop evidence formats and acceptance processes that let independently checked proofs be reused across organizations without hiding assumptions or demanding complete redevelopment.
status: Verified software already reaches real deployments, and CompCert has documented certification-related adoption. The unresolved target is economical, transparent evidence reuse—not initial regulatory acceptance.
why: Reduces duplicated assurance work and rewards reusable verified components.
key_works: CompCert project, 2026 qualification and deployment news; Klein et al. (2018), DOI:10.1145/3230627; Huang et al. (2026), DOI:10.1145/3785652.

title: Independent replication infrastructure for formal-methods claims
subfield: Empirical foundations, datasets, and funding infrastructure
open: Fund and operate repeatable checks of published proofs, solver results, claimed speedups, and toolchain assumptions using archived environments and independently maintained checkers.
status: Artifact evaluation, competitions, and verified checkers supply components; continuous independent replication across the field remains a proposed infrastructure target.
why: Keeps “machine checked” from becoming a claim that cannot be reproduced after publication.
key_works: Carneiro (2026), *Lean4Lean*; Andreotti et al. (2023), *Carcara*; VNN-COMP and SYNTCOMP resources.
